+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan sat in the passenger cabin with his hands folded on his knees and tried to count the crew by the sound of their footsteps. He counted nine. The manifest had listed five. The cabin was small: two chairs bolted to the deck, a scarred metal table, a porthole the size of a dinner plate. Through it, Mars hung like a rusted coin, already shrinking. The man who had brought him aboard, one of the retinue that had come to his home in the polite, unhurried way of people carrying rifles, had said only, "Consul Voss will see you. Please don't touch anything." He had been a mining engineer for twenty years and had never once been invited anywhere. The hatch opened and two people entered. Neither was armed, which was somehow worse. The woman came first. Perhaps fifty, dressed in grey that cost more than Arthur's plot, carrying a folding chair as though it were a precision instrument. Her lapel bore the small starburst insignia he had seen on the retinue's rifles: the Antares diplomatic corp, diplomatic in name only. Behind her came a lean man with a data-slate under one arm and a paper ledger under the other. "Mr. Neegan," said the woman. "I am Consul Voss. This is Mr. Sando, who handles figures. Please sit. Would you like tea? It is real tea, I should mention. We do not do the powdered kind on this ship." "Thank you," Arthur said. "I would rather understand where I am." "You are aboard the *Cassiopeia*, an Antares diplomatic courier, en route to a rendezvous point outside Martian orbit. You will be returned within the day." She set the folding chair down and sat with her hands flat on the table. "You have, it appears, discovered something under your plot." "I have measured something under my plot," Arthur said. "There is a difference, and it matters. The settlement grid flagged my section. The readings were too hot for the local geology, and I am an engineer, so I dug." "Too hot," Voss repeated. "Yes. Azra accelerates radioactive decay. A vein of it large enough to sit under a homestead makes the surrounding rock glow like a furnace. Your plot has been flagged by three separate surveys, two corporate and one belonging to the colony administration." She paused. "The question before us is what happens to a man who owns a furnace." Sando clicked his slate open and began writing. "Projected tonnage," he said, without looking up. "Between nine and eleven thousand tonnes, assuming your geophones were calibrated. I have assumed they were." "They were. I recalibrated them twice." "Then congratulations." Sando turned the page. "Nine thousand tonnes of Azra. A drive core for a colony ship, or the heart of a weapon that could end a war before the declaration was read." Arthur looked at the porthole. Mars was smaller now, a reddish smear against the black. "The lease law," he said. "My plot is freehold. First-generation grant. The corporations can't take it." "Correct. The colonial charter is explicit. That is why we are here instead of a requisition party. The corporations have their own ideas about the law, and the administration has its own, but Antares is in the business of making deals that all parties can sign without a court case." "And what is the deal?" Voss produced a document on heavy paper, creased once like a letter. "We offer to purchase the freehold at a figure Mr. Sando will consider generous, and to assign you and your family to Antares as protected persons. A home. A laboratory, since you are an engineer. A seat at the table when the vein is discussed, because the discoverer has a certain value as a witness, and witnesses who are comfortable are useful witnesses." "And in return?" "An assignment of discovery rights to the Antares Consortium. And a testimony that the vein was found by accident, with no prior knowledge of its extent, no reports to anyone outside your own records." Arthur felt the cabin's cold air on the back of his neck. "You want me to say I didn't know." "We want you to say what is true. You did not know. You measured. There is a difference, and you would do well to remember it." "Who else knows?" "Everyone," said Sando, still writing. "The corporations have been drilling around your section for a month. The administration has a sealed file. The question is who controls the vein when it comes to light, and Antares believes the answer should be: no one alone." "Antares controls the middle," Arthur said. He heard himself say it, and the words surprised him. "You don't want the Azra. You want to be the broker. The corporations pay you, the administration pays you, and nobody can seize the vein without starting a war, because you hold the papers." Voss looked at him for a long moment. Then she smiled, and it was the first genuine thing in the cabin. "Mr. Neegan, you are an engineer. You should be a politician." "I am a mining engineer. I dig things and I measure them. I do not hold papers." "Then consider this," Voss said. "If you refuse, the offer does not expire. It is merely joined by other offers, made by people with less patience for the charter. The corporations are not fond of freeholds that produce weapons. The administration is fond of freeholds only when they are quiet. And there are others, men indentured on Azra leases for ten years, who would not bother with either law." She gathered the tea things with a nod to the steward outside the hatch. "You are not being threatened. You are being given the polite version of a fact." Arthur looked at the document. The figures were real figures, enough to buy every plot in the settlement and still hire the survey drones for a generation. "How long do I have?" "Until we dock back at your station. The *Cassiopeia* is a fast ship. I would not count on the others being equally punctual." The hatch closed behind them, and Arthur sat alone with the drone of the filtration system, which had changed pitch, low and steady, the sound of a ship turning home. Through the porthole, Mars filled the frame again, rust and ice and the thin blue smear of its atmosphere, and somewhere under a modest house on a modest plot, nine thousand tonnes of Azra waited to be found by somebody. He picked up the tea. It was real tea, and it was hot, and it tasted like the only thing in the Solar System that no one had yet put a price on.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Asimovian style and successfully captures the requested retrofuturistic sci-fi atmosphere. The author effectively establishes the political intrigue through dialogue-heavy scenes while maintaining tension throughout Arthur's predicament. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Arthur comes across as a believable everyman engineer thrust into circumstances beyond his control, with his responses feeling authentic to his background. Consul Voss is portrayed as a sophisticated political operator who maintains diplomatic courtesy while delivering veiled threats. The dynamic between these characters drives the narrative effectively. The dialogue carries the story well, revealing character motivations and world-building details naturally. Voss's line "You should be a politician" followed by Arthur's response about being an engineer who "digs things and measures them" effectively establishes their contrasting worldviews. The conversation flows logically and reveals the stakes without excessive exposition. The prose style successfully emulates Asimov's clean, functional approach while incorporating vivid details that enhance rather than overwhelm the narrative. Descriptions like Mars as "a rusted coin" and the Azra vein making rock "glow like a furnace" are evocative without being purple. The technical details about geophones and tonnage feel authentic to the engineering perspective. The world-building operates on multiple levels as requested, from the immediate personal stakes for Arthur to the broader implications of Azra as a strategic resource. The piece effectively hints at larger political machinations involving corporations, colonial administration, and diplomatic corps without overwhelming the reader with exposition. The ending maintains appropriate tension and ambiguity. Arthur's situation remains precarious, and the final image of him drinking real tea - "the only thing in the Solar System that no one had yet put a price on" - provides a moment of bitter irony rather than false comfort. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the dialogue becomes slightly expository, and the pacing could benefit from more varied sentence structures in places. However, these are relatively minor issues in an otherwise well-crafted piece that successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom is the one place on campus where I'm allowed to be bossy without anyone complaining, and tonight I'm bossy about everything. Elliot and I are twelve prints from our final project, and I've got the night running like clockwork: developer at twenty degrees, stop bath fresh, the timer beeping every ten seconds while I work the enlarger. He's nineteen, and he apologizes to the water tap when he bumps it. He came into this class in a lace collar under a paint-splattered denim jacket, boots with three buckles on each, a moth pin on his lapel, and half the room assumed costume. I've watched him all semester, and I can tell you the costume is load-bearing. It's the closest thing he has to a voice. I'm twenty-five. I've dated guys who look like they were carved, sharp jaw, loud opinions, people who could match me for volume. Elliot does the opposite. He's soft. He asks questions that make me stop and reconsider why I do things I've done for years. He's been my favourite person in that classroom since October, and I've been very disciplined about not doing anything about it, because he's nineteen and I don't do things half-assed, even when the thing is just staring at someone's hands. I was getting a fresh stack from the shelf in the wet room when the book I'd been using to prop the door slid off the sill. I heard the door swing before I saw it, and by the time I was back inside, the fluorescents from the corridor were lying flat across the light table. The whole stack, forty sheets, the last of what the department would let us use, was exposed. Foggy grey. Dead. My first move was to fix it. That's what I do. I started mentally reorganizing the semester, the budget, who to call Monday, whether I could talk someone into an override. Elliot just looked at the paper for a long time, then picked one sheet up and held it to the red light, and it was a photograph of nothing. "It's okay," he said. "The negatives are fine. The pictures are still in them." I wanted to argue with him, because I'd already decided this was a disaster. Instead I sat down on the bench, because there was nothing left to do, and the red light did what red light does, made us both the same colour, made faces hard to read. I found myself not reading him, for once, and just listening. "Can I tell you something I haven't told anyone in this class?" he said. I nodded. I didn't say *go ahead, I'm all ears*, because I'm not a person who says that. "The clothes. Everyone assumes the goth thing is a phase or a bit. It's not a bit. But it's not me either. Not exactly. It's what I have. I keep trying on other things in my head, a skirt, shorter hair, other ways of introducing myself, and I don't know if that's me or just the part of me that's scared. I've been reading about people who don't fit the boxes, and I keep coming back to not knowing what box I'm in. I don't know how to say this better. I don't know that there's a better way to say it." I had a whole script ready. That's my problem, I come in with a script. I was about to take charge of it, tell him he was doing fine, tell him what to do next, be the girlfriend who has the plan. I caught myself halfway through the first sentence and put it down instead. Because here's what I didn't expect: I wanted to protect him more than I wanted to lead him. I wanted to wrap the whole confession in something soft and hand it back to him already sorted. And underneath that, something else, I was excited. I'd been circling him for a semester, and this was the first time I felt like I actually knew him. I've always been drawn to people who know exactly what they are. That's my type, and I'm not ashamed of it. Certain. Defined. Someone who looks at me and knows what he wants. Elliot is the opposite of defined, and I can't stop looking at him. He was quiet for a while after that. His fingers worked the edge of a ruined sheet, folding and unfolding it, and I noticed I'd been watching his hands the way I watch a print come up in the developer, not because I want to know the picture yet, but because I know it's coming. "Do you want to hear more," he said, "or do you want to just sit in here with me?" That was new. Nobody asks me what I want. I'm the one who asks everyone else. "Just sit with me," I said. "Okay." He leaned against my shoulder slowly, like he was checking whether I'd let him. I let him. His hand found the negative I was still holding and covered mine on top of it, and neither of us moved it. We sat in the red light for a while, smelling like vinegar and cold water, two people with a ruined stack of paper and a project that now needs a new plan. I could have filled the silence with logistics. I didn't. Some nights the work is the thing, and some nights the work is just the excuse. At midnight he said, "Thursday?" "I'll bring the good developer," I said. At the door I let him go first into the corridor, which is not something I do. I followed him out, and we both had a lot to figure out, and I didn't have the answers, and it turned out I was fine with that.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive 25-year-old while showing her vulnerability when confronted with unexpected feelings. The darkroom setting is used effectively both literally and metaphorically, creating an intimate confessional space that feels authentic to the photography class context. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her natural take-charge personality and her desire to give Elliot agency feels genuine and well-developed. Her observation that "Nobody asks me what I want. I'm the one who asks everyone else" reveals character depth efficiently. Elliot's tentative revelation about gender questioning is handled with sensitivity, avoiding both melodrama and oversimplification. The prose style is clean and purposeful, with strong concrete details like "lace collar under a paint-splattered denim jacket, boots with three buckles on each, a moth pin on his lapel" that establish character efficiently. The metaphor of the ruined photographs works well thematically, representing both vulnerability and potential. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, particularly Elliot's hesitant confession: "I don't know how to say this better. I don't know that there's a better way to say it." This captures the authentic struggle of someone exploring identity without sounding overly polished or therapeutic. However, the piece occasionally relies on telling rather than showing, particularly in establishing Dani's attraction and her typical relationship patterns. Some transitions feel slightly abrupt, and while the ending is appropriately understated, it leaves several emotional threads unresolved in ways that feel incomplete rather than artfully ambiguous. The emotional complexity is well-handled, showing Dani's confusion about her own identity and attraction without making it the central focus. The piece maintains appropriate boundaries around Elliot's vulnerability while still exploring the chemistry between the characters. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma Ben had been standing at the edge of the Trevi Fountain for forty minutes, reading the guidebook aloud to no one, when the scooter came around the corner at roughly illegal speed. It stopped two feet from his face. A woman in a helmet looked down at him over a messenger bag full of parcels, and he looked up with his hands raised, which was worse than nothing. "Scusi!" he said. "Scusi, scusi!" She looked at him. She looked at the guidebook skidding across the wet travertine. "You stand in the middle of the road with a book," she said, in Italian, then in English, then in Italian again, laughing. "You are standing inside the museum and reading the map." "I am very sorry," he said. "Is there damage? I have a card." She took the card, studied it, flipped it back to him. "No damage. Lucky you." "Grazie," he said, bowing slightly, because he was that kind of man. "You don't thank me," she said. "I nearly hit you." His pen skidded across the travertine alongside the guidebook, and she caught it out of the air, which was the first of several things she would do without asking. Her scooter had a long scratch across the tank painted over in hot pink, and a dent near the kickstand wearing a sticker of a smiling sun. "What happened there?" he asked, pointing, because he did not know what else to do. "A story," she said. "For when you've earned it. I'm Alessandra. I deliver things." Her phone buzzed. She glanced at it, then at him, and did something he would spend the next six hours trying to explain to people. "I have forty minutes before my next order," she said. "Come with me." He said he had a schedule. He was a lecturer on sabbatical, which in his department meant he was supposed to be writing and in Rome meant he was standing at fountains. He had a hotel with a checkout time. She was already swinging a leg over the scooter. "Rome has been waiting two thousand years," she said. "It can wait for your notes." He did not go. He went. He sat behind her with his hands on the leather where a rain guard used to be, and she peeled away from the fountain into a street so narrow that tourists would have needed a map, and took it at speed anyway, hooting at a man taking a selfie of an obelisk. "Hold on, Professore." The wind took his glasses; he put them back on crooked and laughed, which was new. She drove through a market, up a ramp, across a bridge he did not recognize. "Why are you doing this?" he shouted over the engine. "Because I am a troublemaker," she shouted back. "It's in my contract. This is not a tour. Tours are for people who pay." She stopped at a stall where a man was selling bread and cheese and pretending, with great commitment, not to see her. She took a baguette and a wedge of pecorino. "The stall owner knows me," she said. "We have an arrangement." She handed him half the bread. "Non guardare, mangia. Don't look, eat." He ate it standing up, feeling ridiculous, and noticed she had also lifted a small bronze key from a hook on the wall and put it in her pocket. He decided, for reasons he could not have articulated, to say nothing. At a dead end she hopped a wall without slowing down. He stood there with bread crumbs on his shirt until she turned back, grabbed the front of his jacket, and hauled him up by sheer force. "You'd break a hip," she said. "Professore is not built for Rome." She took him up a staircase that belonged to nobody, past a shuttered church, to a ledge above the rooftops where the whole city lay out like a board game. She sat with her legs dangling. He stood back, too polite to sit on the edge. "Professore is afraid of heights," she said. "No," he said. "I am afraid of you." That made her laugh, a real laugh. She held out her phone. "Sit. I'm taking a photo." He sat halfway, arms braced, and in the photo she looked like she owned the city and he looked like a man being introduced to it. "Do you do this often?" he asked. "Take people on tours?" "Only the ones worth stealing time for." At the Tiber, she found stones the color of olives. She skipped four, five, six. The water was green and warm and smelled of the city's history, which is to say, of nothing in particular. "Your turn," she said. "No," he said. "Professore is afraid of the water." "Afraid is not in your vocabulary here either," she said. He threw a stone. It sank with the dignity of a stone that had given up. She splashed him with both hands, and he got soaked and did not wipe it off. "You're having fun," she said. It was not a question, and it was not quite a compliment either. "I haven't had fun in years," he said, which was a stupid thing to say, and he watched her face do something complicated for half a second. Then she was flicking pebbles at his feet again. "Everyone says that," she said. "It's a tourist thing." She dropped him outside his hotel in the late afternoon, when the city had gone gold. He stood there with wet hair and no idea what to do with the rest of his day. "Where should I go tomorrow?" he asked, because he was a man who needed to know where to go. She reached into his messenger bag without asking and took out the guidebook. Then she held up his pen, which she had caught out of the air that morning and never once given back. "Piazza Navona," she said, writing on the back cover in handwriting that slanted like it was running away. "Ten o'clock. If you want to see me." She held out the guidebook and the pen together. He took the guidebook. She put the pen in her pocket. "Keep it," she said. "I have enough." Then she was gone, down the street, the pink scratch on the tank catching the light, and Ben stood outside his hotel holding a book with an address on it, and for the first time in his life, he did not check whether the address was real.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested contemporary romance structure. The narrative successfully captures the cultural clash between Ben, the polite British academic, and Alessandra, the impulsive Roman courier, through well-observed details and natural dialogue that reveals character rather than exposition. The writing exhibits confident prose with memorable phrases like "Rome has been waiting two thousand years. It can wait for your notes" and "he looked like a man being introduced to it." The author skillfully weaves in Alessandra's kleptomania through subtle actions - taking the pen, lifting the bronze key, keeping the pen at the end - without heavy-handed exposition. This shows sophisticated storytelling technique. Character development feels authentic, particularly Ben's gradual loosening from his rigid academic persona. His progression from apologetic tourist to someone who "did not check whether the address was real" feels earned through the day's experiences. Alessandra maintains her enigmatic quality while showing glimpses of depth, especially in her momentary reaction when Ben admits he hasn't had fun in years. The pacing moves effectively through distinct scenes - the fountain encounter, the impromptu tour, the rooftop view, the river stones - each building their connection while maintaining narrative momentum. The dialogue feels natural and character-specific, avoiding stilted romance tropes. However, some elements could be stronger. While the cultural differences are well-established, Ben's transformation, though gradual, pushes believability slightly. The piece occasionally relies on convenient coincidences, and some of Alessandra's more daring actions (like the wall-hopping) feel somewhat performative rather than organic to character. The ending strikes an appropriate note of possibility without forced resolution, leaving tension unresolved in a way that serves the larger narrative structure requested. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Last Outpost smells like ozone and burnt honey, which is mostly the Vega whisky, mostly the air scrubbers, and a little bit Brix, who has been sweating into the same jacket since Tuesday. "Same as always?" I ask. "Same as always," he says, and I slide him his cup of something brown and strong that I don't label because nobody asks. Evenings here run on a rhythm I've kept for six years now. Brix complains about ore grades. Odile trades gossip at a rate that would embarrass a courier. Somebody's love life needs arbitrating, somebody's docking fee needs arguing down, somebody's got a hangover that needs a towel and a kind word. I keep the peace the way I keep the glasses, upright, in rows, wiped until they catch the lamp light. It's a good life. It's a small life, but it's mine, and the belt is big enough that nobody remembers what mine used to be. The bell over the door gives a tired little chime, and a stranger drops onto the stool at the far end of the bar like a sack of ore. Frazzled is the wrong word, but it's the closest one I have. Their coat is scorched along one shoulder. Their hair, if you can call it hair, is a nest of long filaments coiled into dread-like strands, and half of them are hanging loose and askew, one trailing down their forearm like a dropped glove. They look like they've been through a fire and then a fight with a door. "Vega whisky, neat," they say. "Better make that a double." I pour. As I set the glass down, their elbow clips the rail and a spare glass slides off the ledge and breaks against the floor, a bright little crackle that makes Brix flinch. I don't look up. I sweep the shards into my hand without pausing my pour, because I've been doing this a long time and my hands learned before my eyes did. "You're quick," the stranger says. "You're a customer," I say. "I don't want you bleeding on the bar." They drink half the double in one go. The loose filaments twitch, settling, the way a dog's ears do when it hears something far off. "Three systems behind me," they say. "And counting." "Behind you where?" "Wherever the Guild points its little finger." They take another pull. "Kestrel claim. Shaft collapse. Eleven crew, four still in the med-bay at home." Odile, three stools down, goes very still. She's been mid-sentence about a freighter dispute and just stops, like the words got yanked out of her. "That's the one," she says quietly. "That's the one who pulled the maintenance logs." "Odile," the stranger says, and their voice has gone flat and careful. "I'd rather we didn't." "You blew the logs off the company servers, Tarn. The Guild posted a bounty. The company posted a bigger one." She turns to me, and I watch her do the math I know she's doing. She has contracts with that company. She docks her freighter in their hangar. "Nets, you understand what this is." "I understand there's a man with a whisky problem sitting at my bar," I say. "That's the part I understand." "Then understand he's sitting in the one place they'll look." "Everywhere's a place they'll look. That's not my problem. My problem is he's spilling on my floor." Tarn laughs, a short broken thing. "Fair. Sorry about the glass. Sorry about the floor. Sorry about the coat, probably. Everything's on fire behind me and I keep finding new ways to scorch the furniture." "Where's the fire?" I ask. "The company's saying the collapse was crew error. Maintenance error would have meant they owed eleven families. So the logs went missing, and then I went missing, and now I'm here." They gesture at the Outpost with their glass. "You've got a scanner out front. Ships register in and out. You'd know if one of theirs came through." "I'd know," I say. "I'd know the way I know Brix is sweating." Brix, who has been pretending not to listen for two minutes, raises a hand. "What company?" "Does it matter to your ore grades?" Odile says. "It matters if they're docking my claim too." "It doesn't matter to anyone here," Tarn says, and now their voice is different, tighter, the voice of someone who has decided to be a stranger again. "Nobody here knows my name. Nobody here saw me come through. I'll be gone before your shift change, Nets. That's the deal." "And if they're already through?" The question hangs there. Outside, the belt turns in the dark, patient as ever, full of ships that don't ask questions. Tarn looks at me for a long moment. Then they look at the double, and the double is empty, and their filaments have gone still, all of them, like a held breath. "Tell me you have a back room," they say. I look at Odile. She looks at the door, then at me, and her expression says very plainly: *choose, and choose slowly.* I look at the shelf behind me, where the glasses stand in their rows, catching the light, and I think about how I've spent six years keeping everything upright. The scanner out front chimes, soft and polite, the sound it makes when a ship registers at the dock. Then it chimes again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested cozy sci-fi atmosphere. The author successfully establishes Nets as a compelling first-person narrator with a distinct voice - pragmatic, observant, and protective of the sanctuary she's built. Her dialogue feels natural and reveals character efficiently, particularly in lines like "I understand there's a man with a whisky problem sitting at my bar" which shows her deliberate choice to focus on immediate, manageable problems rather than larger conflicts. The world-building is economical but effective, establishing the asteroid belt setting through sensory details like "ozone and burnt honey" and character behaviors rather than exposition dumps. The author creates a lived-in feeling through small details like Brix's perpetually worn jacket and the established rhythms of evening service. The conflict introduction feels organic - Tarn's arrival and the revelation about the mining accident creates genuine tension without feeling forced. The dialogue carries most of the narrative weight as requested, and conversations feel authentic to each character's position and motivations. Odile's shift from gossip to calculating self-interest when she recognizes Tarn demonstrates nuanced character work. The prose style is clean and purposeful, avoiding overwrought descriptions while still creating atmosphere. Metaphors like comparing Tarn's arrival to "a sack of ore" feel appropriate to the setting. The pacing builds tension effectively toward the scanner chimes ending, which provides a strong cliffhanger without resolving the central conflict. However, some elements could be stronger. While the characters are distinct, they don't reach full complexity within this chapter's scope. The conflict, while well-introduced, follows fairly predictable patterns of corporate malfeasance and whistleblower pursuit. The emotional stakes, while present, could dig deeper into what this sanctuary means to Nets and why she might risk it. The writing occasionally relies on familiar genre tropes (corrupt mining company, missing maintenance logs) though it executes them competently. The piece maintains consistent quality throughout without major weaknesses in craft or structure. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South** The saxophone finds me first. It comes out of somewhere near the cathedral, low and golden, rolling over the crowd on Royal Street like it owns the whole block. I can feel it in my sternum, which is a fact, not a metaphor. It's ten in the morning and I'm standing in New Orleans with a dead phone, fourteen dollars, two granola bars, and a hoodie I'll need later, and I have been here one hour and I still don't believe it. Two days ago I told my family I was a girl. That's the version with soft edges. The real version: I came out on a Tuesday, my mother called the school counsellor, the counsellor called her back and used the phrase "concerning behavioural patterns," and my father said the word *confused* so many times I started counting it. Forty-eight hours of that, a kitchen table that got smaller every day, my mother's eyes doing this thing where she looked through me like I was a window. So last night I made a plan in about thirty minutes, backpack, hoodie, forty-four dollars, and I stood on the road until a truck with tinted windows slowed down. I paid him thirty dollars for the ride. He still threw me out in downtown New Orleans, honked once, and drove off like I was a stain on the seat. So here I am. Free, apparently. Which is a funny feeling, like being dropped off the edge of something and discovering you can't swim yet. The heat is the first thing the city does to you. It's not like Tennessee heat, where you can at least feel the air moving. This is a wet towel held over your face. The crowd is thick with tourists, camera straps, sunburns, people eating ice cream that melts into their hands. A woman in a sundress stops me and asks if I'm lost. I say no. She says I look like I'm in the wrong neighborhood for a kid walking alone, and I say I'm not alone, and she smiles like she knows better and keeps going. I'm hungry in a way that has a physical location, right behind my sternum, competing with the saxophone. "You're new," a voice says. "Backpack, no destination, eyes doing the scan." She's sitting on a bench outside a bakery, splitting a sandwich that's been in a bag long enough to have opinions. She's got a stolen-looking jacket, a phone that's too nice, and a grin that arrives before her sentences do. She's maybe seventeen. She says eighteen. I don't know if I believe that either. "June," she says. "You look like you haven't eaten since Memphis." "I haven't." "Here." She hands me half the sandwich. It's stale and cold and I eat it like it's a medal. "Okay," she says, watching me. "Now you owe me. Not money. Answers. Where you from?" "Tennessee." "Runaway?" "Does it look like I ran?" "It looks like you got thrown out of a truck, which is a more specific kind of runaway." She laughs at her own joke and takes a bite, and I notice her sleeve is pulled down over her forearm even though it's ninety degrees and she's already sweating. I tell her the story. Not all of it. The comeout, the forty-eight hours, the truck. I leave out the part where I cried in a gas station bathroom for twenty minutes because I was scared and proud at the same time, which is a combination nobody warns you about. June listens with her mouth full, nodding like I'm entertaining her. Then she says, "You should know something about this place." I sit down. I'm too hungry to stand. "The Quarter is beautiful and it eats people. There are guys on these streets who can tell you've run away in about ten seconds flat. They're not after your money. Your money is nothing. They're after the fact that you're scared and you've got nowhere else and nobody's looking for you." She points at me with a piece of bread. "You're the easiest target in this whole city right now. Everyone here knows it." "Everyone?" "The musicians, the vendors, the guys who sell fake watches. They all know who's new and who's staying. It's like a weather system." She shrugs. "I've been here since April." "Since April. From where?" "Doesn't matter." "That's a weird thing to say to someone who just told you everything." "Everything's not everything," she says. "I'll tell you what matters. There's a spot under the bridge by the river where it's cooler at night and nobody asks questions. I'll show you tonight. But you don't get to ask where I'm from. That's the deal." I want to say no. The alarm bells are going, and I know it, I can feel them buzzing behind my ears. She's too smooth. She's too eager. She's giving me food and a place to sleep and I have nothing to offer in return except half a sandwich and a story she didn't want. Then I notice the way she keeps glancing at the street, and the way her whole body goes stiff when a black SUV with tinted windows rolls past, and I think: okay. She's running from something too. That doesn't make her safe. But it makes her one of the few people in this city who knows what I know. "Also," she says, "for the record. I take things. From people with more than me. Not from kids. Not from runaways. You're safe on that front." "Thanks for the heads-up." "Anytime." We walk. The sun gets lower and the light goes gold on the old brick and the crowd thins from tourists to locals, and the saxophone comes back, this time closer, a man in a suit with a brass case playing something slow and sad outside a bar, and for a second I'm not a runaway. I'm just a person on a street in a city older than my country, listening to music. That's the thing about this place. It keeps trying to make you feel like you belong. I don't know if that's a kindness or a trap. At nightfall June stops under the bridge. The river is dark and wide and smells like mud and money, and the concrete is cool under my sneakers, which is the first cool thing I've touched all day. "So," she says. "You can stay here tonight, or you can keep walking. Your call." "Your call," I say. "You offered." "Offers expire." I think about the bus stop back downtown. The honk of the truck that dropped me. My mother's eyes doing the window thing. I think about June's pulled sleeve and her stiff shoulders and her stolen jacket and the fact that she split her sandwich with me without being asked, which is either generosity or the first move of a con I haven't figured out yet. "Okay," I say. "But I'm asking your name for real." "June." "Real name?" She looks at me for a long second, and I can see her deciding. "Real name." I sit down on the cool concrete. The saxophone is still playing somewhere up the bank, and the streetlights come on one by one along the river, and I'm sixteen and I'm tired and I'm following a girl who admits she steals. I choose her anyway, because the alternative is the dark, and I've been alone long enough.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and authentic voice work. The author successfully captures Taylor's perspective as a transgender teen runaway with genuine emotional complexity - the mixture of fear, pride, desperation, and cautious hope feels earned rather than manufactured. The first-person narration maintains consistency throughout, with Taylor's voice feeling appropriately young but not artificially so. The prose quality is notably high, with evocative sensory details that ground the reader in New Orleans without becoming overly descriptive. Lines like "the saxophone finds me first" and "heat is the first thing the city does to you" establish atmosphere efficiently. The writing avoids purple prose while still being literary and engaging. Character development is nuanced, particularly in the portrayal of June. She's presented as simultaneously helpful and potentially dangerous, with clear hints at her own troubled background (the covered sleeve, reaction to the SUV, admission of theft). This creates appropriate tension without making her cartoonishly mysterious. Taylor's internal conflict about trusting June feels psychologically realistic for someone in their situation. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, revealing character through speech patterns and what characters choose to reveal or withhold. June's casual admission "I take things. From people with more than me" is particularly well-crafted - it's honest without being overly dramatic. The pacing works well, covering Taylor's first day while building toward the decision to trust June. The ending avoids false optimism while providing a moment of connection that feels earned given the circumstances. Taylor's final choice is presented as pragmatic rather than naive - they acknowledge the risks but choose companionship over isolation. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly self-conscious, and a few descriptions that edge toward being overly polished for a distressed teenager's perspective. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The piece successfully adheres to the prompt requirements, incorporating the requested elements (meeting another runaway, navigating trust issues, internal monologue, mixed tense) while maintaining narrative coherence. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The predicament, as Midas saw it, was that there was one tin of peaches left, and that the well water tasted like the well had been thinking about iron. "Sit," said Chewy. "Let us deliberate." Chewy was an animo-tronic, which meant he was a stuffed koala with the mechanical ambition of a much larger animal. He had come from the before time, a long time ago, when people made things that moved and spoke, and then stopped making things that moved and spoke, and the world had to learn to be quiet again. His battery read 44 percent, which he considered a forecast rather than a crisis. "The mission," said Midas, "is food. The Old Town is where the food would be, if the Old Town still had food, which it probably didn't, because the Old Town had been sitting there for three hundred years with its doors open and its pockets turned out." "Agreed," said Chewy. "Also, my ears have not been oiled in some time. I can hear a bee from a mile, which is a talent I did not ask for." They left at dawn, because dawn was when trouble was least likely to have noticed them yet. The first route to the Old Town was the road, and the road was gone, in the sense that a quarter mile of it had decided to become a hole. They stood at the edge of the hole and looked down at the road continuing, cheerfully, at the bottom. "Bridge," said Chewy. "There was a bridge." "Was," said Midas. They went back the way they came, which was a way of saying the first mission had lasted forty minutes and produced a view of a hole. Chewy's left button eye worked loose on the way back and came to rest in Midas's pocket, where it felt like a coin, which was a pity, because nothing Midas touched had ever turned to gold or anything else of value. The second route was across the fields, longer but without holes at the edges. It was also, it turned out, the route that went through the culvert. The culvert was a hole in the ground with a roof, which seemed like an improvement, until Midas stepped in it. The culvert had no bottom, which is not a design feature one expects from a culvert, but the before time had been generous with its surprises. Midas sank to his waist, and the water was cold and had opinions about his trousers. "Chewy," he said. "Chewy, I am in a culvert." "Your trousers," said Chewy, "are now part of the culvert." Chewy lowered himself in, a heroic act given his battery, and hauled Midas out by the collar, which left the trousers in the culvert and the dignity somewhere along the road. They crawled the rest of the way home, which was a way of getting home no one had ever described as dignified, but was at least efficient. The third time out, they took the long way along the ridge, because Midas had decided holes were a conspiracy and Chewy had decided holes were a statistical certainty, but that the ridge was worth trying. It was on the ridge that they found the graffiti, on the wall of a house that had been a house in the before time and was now mostly a wall. In paint faded to the colour of a promise, someone had written: SEEK REFUGE WHERE THE PINE FELL Below it was an arrow, pointing into the wilds. "Refuge," said Midas. "That's a real word. That's a word that means somewhere you go when things are bad." "Or somewhere you go when things are very bad," said Chewy. "The before time used such words on signs near things that were not, in the end, refuges. 'Dead end.' 'This way to the exit.' It was not a society that always told the truth." But the arrow pointed into the wilds, and the wilds were where the pine would have fallen, and the tin of peaches was still at home, and so they followed the arrow. They found the pine. It had fallen across a clearing and lain there for centuries, and the centuries had done what centuries do, which was to grow moss on it and make it look like a bench nobody was allowed to sit on. Beyond it, set into the hillside and half-swallowed by ferns, was a door. The door was steel, with a wheel, and it was open about as far as a door gets open when it has been open for three hundred years and the hinges have given up on everything except the concept of opening. They went in. Inside was a room. The room had a chair, a kettle, and a notice board, and the notice board was laminated, which meant somebody had once cared about notice boards, and that was, in its way, a comfort. The top notice read: THE REFUGE IS CLOSED FOR RENOVATIONS. ESTIMATED REOPENING: 2087. Below it were older notices. One was about a lost dog. One about a lost cat. And one, yellowed and curling, read: LOST: KOALA, ANSWERS TO CHEWY. LAST SEEN: [illegible]. If found, please return. Reward: a hug. Chewy looked at the notice for a long time. "Would you like a hug?" he said, eventually, to no one in particular. They went back out, and the door stayed open behind them, which felt like the refuge had let them out of kindness, or out of indifference, and it was hard to tell the difference. The return home took the long way, because the ridge was the only way that was not a hole. Midas wore one boot, the other having been left behind in the culvert with the trousers. Chewy's battery read 3 percent, and his ears, un-oiled and heroic, could hear the farmhouse from a mile, and he was right about that too, because the farmhouse was there when they arrived: leaking, familiar, and worse for wear, along with everyone in it. They sat by the fire with the tin of peaches between them, unopened, because opening it would have made the day a success, and the day had not been a success. "The graffiti was accurate," said Midas. "The refuge is in the wilds." "It is," said Chewy. "It is closed for renovations. Until 2087." "Which is a long time." "By the standards of the before time, yes. By the standards of a pine tree, it is a weekend." Chewy's battery read 2 percent. His servos had begun to slow, and his opinions were now delivered at roughly the speed of a glacier, which was still faster than the before time had managed with its bureaucracy. "Tomorrow," said Chewy, "we try the Old Town again. Perhaps the hole will have filled in." "Or," said Midas, "we eat the peaches." "Tomorrow," said Chewy, "we try the Old Town again. I am a creature of mission." And the fire burned, and the roof leaked, and the tin of peaches sat between them like a small golden promise of a day that had not yet happened, which was more than the day that had just happened could claim.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive voice and style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical observations, and gentle absurdism effectively. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both melancholic and oddly comforting, populated by characters who maintain dignity despite their circumstances. The story structure follows the prompt precisely: deliberation, mission planning, multiple failures, and return home worse for wear. The three failed attempts (hole in road, culvert mishap, closed refuge) create a satisfying pattern of escalating disappointment that feels authentically Pratchettian. Midas and Chewy are well-developed characters with distinct voices. Midas embodies hapless determination while Chewy provides mechanical wisdom delivered with koala-appropriate gravity. Their dialogue feels natural and serves both character development and plot advancement. The relationship between them is touching without being sentimental. The prose demonstrates considerable skill in mimicking Pratchett's style - the philosophical asides about holes, time, and bureaucracy; the matter-of-fact treatment of absurd situations; the gentle humor that emerges from character rather than forced jokes. Sentences like "the culvert had no bottom, which is not a design feature one expects from a culvert" perfectly capture this tone. The imagery is vivid and economical, painting a clear picture of this post-technological world without over-description. The refuge sequence, particularly the discovery of Chewy's missing poster, provides genuine emotional weight without manipulation. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - they return unsuccessful but not defeated, maintaining hope without false optimism. The unopened tin of peaches serves as an effective symbol of deferred satisfaction and persistent hope. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the Pratchett pastiche feels slightly forced, and some descriptions could be more precise. However, these are small flaws in an otherwise accomplished piece that successfully fulfills its ambitious brief. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The rain came in sideways off the harbour, and Carys was halfway through shelving the new arrivals when the door opened and a man came through it like he'd been waiting all day for an excuse to stop running. He was tall, soaked to the waist, wearing a coat that had cost more than her van. Through the window she could see them: three figures on the pavement with umbrellas, one of them holding a lens long enough to reach into the next parish. "Bless me," he said. "You've saved my life." "I've saved your shoes, if anything. Doormat's by the till." He laughed, and it was a big laugh, the kind that had been rehearsed in front of mirrors and audiences, but it landed anyway. He shook his hair like a dog and looked around the shop with genuine delight. "Is this real? A bookshop? In Wales?" "It's real. Wales is real. It's raining, which is also real." "God, I love this. I've been followed through four countries this week and nobody has ever offered me a doormat. What do you do with all that paper, by the way?" "Sell some of it." "Brilliant. Tell me you stock the classics." "Stock everything. Classics, cookery, a book on sheep, which sells." He grinned at that, and Carys felt the grin hit her somewhere under her ribs and she was annoyed about it immediately. She turned back to the shelves. "You know, I'm Dane," he said. "Dane Whitlock. I did *The Long Dark*." Carys didn't turn around. "Dane Whitlock." A pause. "*The Long Dark*." "Seen it?" "I've seen the poster. It was in the butcher's window. There was a man in it looking very sad near a cliff." He was quiet for a moment, and she could feel him recalibrating, the way a man adjusts his tie after someone's looked through him. "Fair enough," he said. "Fair enough. The village did the heavy lifting." He wandered the aisles, touching spines, and she watched him do it from the till, which was not a sensible thing to be watching him do. "Can I ask you something?" he said, coming back. "Do you ever get tired of being nobody?" "I get tired of being busy. Nobody's a job description." "Right. Right. And what do you do with your evenings, then? When the shutters go down?" "Television. A dog. Sometimes I walk the headland." "You walk the headland." He said it slowly, like he was tasting it. "That's a lovely thing to do. I do that sort of thing, when I can. Which is never." "Then don't do it when you can't." He laughed again, but smaller this time. He leaned against the shelf of paperbacks and looked at her properly for the first time, and she had the distinct impression that he was deciding whether she was worth being charming at, and she hoped, for reasons she refused to examine, that the answer was yes. "Here's the truth," he said. "After the premiere, I went to a bar in Bristol. No one knew me. I sat there for an hour and nobody wanted a photo, nobody wanted an opinion, nobody wanted anything. And I felt like a man coming up for air." He rubbed the back of his neck. "The thing is, I don't know who I am in that room. I've never been in a room without an audience. It's terrifying, being nobody. I'm not saying that to be pitied. I'm saying it because you look like someone who's never had that problem, and I want to know what it's like." Carys picked up a receipt roll and started tearing it into squares. "It's quiet," she said. "That's all. You're in it, and it's quiet, and you get on with things." "And you're not lonely in it?" "Sometimes. Being famous can't be much different." He looked at her as though she'd handed him a coin he couldn't spend. "That's the first honest thing anyone's said to me in a week." "Good. Try to stay out of the way of the cameras then." Outside, the umbrellas were moving along the pavement, and the rain had dropped to a drizzle. He checked his phone, saw something, and sighed. "They'll be back at the B&B by now. I should go before they realise I've gone." "Then go." "Wait." He was already at the till. "You said you'd recommend something to a man who's read everything and remembers nothing." "I didn't say that." "You implied it. I'm asking anyway." She went to the shelf and pulled down a slim blue volume. "A book about lighthouses. The keeper's diary from the headland, actually. Nineteen-forties. He writes about the weather, the oil, the seals. He never once writes about who was looking at his light." He took it, read the cover, and put a ten-pound note on the glass. "Will you be back in the village?" she asked, before she could decide not to. "No idea. The press will decide." "Then I suppose you'll be back in the shop by accident." He smiled, and this time it didn't reach his mouth first. "By accident," he agreed. "Thank you for the silence, Carys." He left before she could stop herself from saying anything more, and the rain closed behind him like a curtain. She stood at the till a moment, holding the ten pounds, then found the receipt roll she'd been tearing, and underneath it, where he'd signed for the book, a small line in his looping hand: *Thank you for the silence.* She folded it twice and put it in the drawer with the loose change, where the rain couldn't reach it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Dane's performative charm gradually giving way to vulnerability, and Carys's dry, grounded responses that mask her growing interest. The Welsh setting is effectively established through subtle details like the harbour, headland, and local references without becoming heavy-handed. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with each character's personality emerging through their speech patterns. Dane's initial theatrical charm ("Bless me, you've saved my life") contrasts well with Carys's pragmatic responses ("I've saved your shoes, if anything"). The author skillfully shows Dane's fragile ego through his recalibration when his fame doesn't impress her, and his honest confession about not knowing who he is without an audience. The romantic chemistry builds naturally through their verbal sparring, with Carys's immunity to his charm paradoxically drawing him in. Her internal conflict is well-handled - she's clearly affected by him but maintains her defenses. The moment where she asks if he'll be back reveals her interest despite herself. The prose is generally elegant with some particularly strong moments like "the rain closed behind him like a curtain" and the lighthouse book serving as effective symbolism. The pacing works well, building from his dramatic entrance to their more intimate conversation. However, there are some minor weaknesses. Certain phrases feel slightly overwrought ("hit her somewhere under her ribs"), and a few moments border on being too neat in their symbolism. The ending, while touching, risks being somewhat predictable in its romantic setup. Some of Dane's dialogue occasionally feels a bit constructed rather than entirely natural, though this could be intentional given his performative nature. The piece successfully avoids major pitfalls like unearned transformations or incongruent positivity. The characters remain consistent throughout, and their attraction develops believably within the constraints of a single scene. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave with a sound like a whale's knuckle, and Aya stepped down into the dark of the underhold, Katra's shoulder pressed to her back, Simeon's lantern held low. Too quiet. That was the first wrongness. The upper guild should have been drunk on the news of the arrest, shouting over cards and cheap gin. Instead: tar and coal, condensation dripping off whale-oil pipes, brine rising through the floorboards of the old whaling station the Morska had bought out of the Crown. "The spell-lock's brass is warm," Simeon said, keeping his lantern low. "Warm means it's been opened tonight." "By whom?" Katra asked, and the two of them looked at Aya, who did not answer, because she was already thinking about her mother, who had once stood at the edge of a secret and learned the other side. Then the lamps came on. Not the lanterns. Lamps, a dozen of them in brass sockets along the wall, lit in a single instant, as though by a hand that had decided the dark was finished. At the foot of the stair stood Vesper Morska in an oiled canvas coat, a Webley revolver loose at her side, and behind her two men with carbines whose barrels found the three of them before Aya had finished turning. "Close the door," Vesper said. The door closed. "Now you've all three wasted a very good night." "The papers this morning were accurate," Vesper said, stepping up the stairs the way a captain walks a deck. "I was arrested. I was not, it appears, kept." "You staged it," Simeon said. "You let them take you, then left the guild to tear itself apart, waiting to see who would climb." "I let them take me," Vesper agreed, "and I left a guild to discover that a leader is a chair, and chairs are easy to sit in and easy to knock over." She looked at Katra, then at Simeon, and finally at Aya. "Here's the one who climbed fastest." Katra moved first. That was the mistake. The carbine butt took her across the temple with a sound like a fist on a barrel, and she went down without a word. Simeon raised his hands, which Aya respected, because Simeon knew when a fight had already been lost. Aya did not raise hers. She reached for the immateria, the cold country behind her eyelids, and found it sluggish, thick, turned to syrup by the fear in her own blood. She got nothing but a flicker, a black oiling at the edge of her vision, and Vesper watched it the way a man watches a candle gutter. "Immateria," Vesper said. "So the rumor had teeth." The mask came off next, taken by a guard who was not gentle, and Aya let it happen. There was no use in dignity. Her face, pale, aristocratic, marked along the knuckles by the faint grey tracery her mother had left her, lay out under the lamps. "Odile's girl," Vesper said. "You were seven when they hanged her. I remember. I was in the crowd." The cold that came then was not the immateria's. It was ordinary, human cold. "You knew her," Aya said. "Knew her. Employed her. Paid her three years to keep Morska shipments through customs without a clerk ever seeing a shadow. When the magistrate came sniffing, someone had to be the shadow's source. Odile was cheap to name and worth more dead than alive. I am not proud of it. I am not sorry either." "Then you want me dead too," Aya said. "For the same arithmetic." "I want the artifact in that vault, and I want to know what's behind the veil you've been fishing out of it. The Crown calls magick a capital crime. I call it cargo. Your mother was cargo that got loose. You are cargo that came to me on its own." Simeon, from the floor, said, "And if we don't talk?" "Then you three are found in the harbor with your boots full of ballast, and the papers say the arrest went badly for the guild and no one asks questions." Vesper produced a ledger from her coat. "I keep accounts. Odile's column was closed a long time ago. Yours is open." Aya's wrists were bound with tarred cord. She could not fight, could not flee, could not summon anything stronger than a guttering wick. But she had one asset left, and it was herself. "You need me alive," she said. "You've got the key and the spell-lock, but no idea how to open the immateria properly. If I'm found hanged in the harbor, the Ashcombe estate asks questions, and questions about the Morska have a way of reaching the Admiralty." Vesper was quiet long enough that the foghorn sounded three times in the harbor beyond the guild walls, slow, brass-throated, marking the night like a clerk's pen. "Your mother could have bargained too," Vesper said at last. "She chose the rope's silence." "Your mother was afraid," Aya said. "I've had twelve years to study what fear does to a magick user. It makes them small." She let the immateria leak, just a little, a black oiling of the air between them, cold and hungry. "You want the gift. I am the gift. Kill me and it drowns with me, and you're left with a vault door you can't open and a rumor you can't prove." "Teach me," Vesper said. "You live, you work, you stay in the underhold where the lamps are always lit and the door always locked, and in a year I will have what your mother had. Katra and Simeon get their boots back. You get a name on my payroll." Aya looked at the vault door, warm brass, humming gold, the Scythian thing inside turning slowly in the dark like a coin being weighed. "Terms," she said. "In writing. And my mother's column, closed." Vesper smiled for the first time, and it was the smile of a ship that had found its cargo. "Done," she said, and signed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully incorporating all requested story beats while maintaining the specified whalepunk Victorian aesthetic. The author creates an atmospheric underground setting with effective worldbuilding details like whale-oil pipes, tarred cord, and brass fixtures that reinforce the maritime industrial theme. The dialogue feels authentic to the gritty Victorian setting, with characters speaking in measured, formal tones that suit their criminal underworld context. Vesper's revelation about betraying Aya's mother is particularly well-handled, delivered with cold pragmatism that establishes her as a compelling antagonist. The negotiation sequence builds tension effectively as Aya leverages her aristocratic status and magical abilities. Character motivations remain consistent throughout. Vesper's staged arrest and calculated manipulation feel believable for a guild leader, while Aya's quick thinking under pressure aligns with her established intelligence and magical heritage. The power dynamics shift naturally as information is revealed. The prose maintains an appropriate tone without becoming overwrought. Descriptions like "a sound like a whale's knuckle" and "the smile of a ship that had found its cargo" enhance the maritime atmosphere without feeling forced. The pacing moves efficiently through the confrontation without unnecessary meandering. However, some elements feel somewhat predictable - the staged arrest and the negotiation for survival follow familiar patterns. The magical system could be more clearly defined, as the immateria's limitations seem convenient to the plot. The ending, while logical, resolves perhaps too neatly given the high stakes established. The emotional complexity is solid but not exceptional. Aya's internal conflict about her mother's fate and her own predicament creates genuine tension, though deeper exploration of her psychological state could strengthen the piece. The gothic horror elements are present but understated.
