+ Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The spot on the counter I keep wiping sits right where Maro sets his glass, and it has been the same spot for nine years, which tells you something about me. Third week running, Kess and Ivo have been doing their thing. Kess wants Ivo to stop trading ore with her sister. Ivo wants Kess to stop calling it a betrayal when it's a business arrangement. I slide them each a glass of something cheap and tell them the belt's been quiet long enough that they should be grateful for any argument that doesn't involve a lawsuit. Maro laughs, which settles it. This is my evening. This is the whole point. I left a life with a name on it. Here I'm Nets, and people tolerate my habit of absorbing everyone's problems because I pour good drinks and remember their mothers' names. Then the stranger plops down at the bar. Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double. She's a vire, I think, or something related. Tentacles braided into dreads, the way their kind does, except hers hang loose and matted, ship dust in the strands. Everyone knows a vire's braids come undone when they're scared. I've seen it once before, at a funeral, and I didn't like what it looked like. I pour the double. It sweats immediately. "Double's for a bad day or a worse one," I say. "Both." She drinks half of it in one pull, which is a lot for anyone, and then sets the glass down flat, both tentacle-hands braced on the bar like she's checking the floor won't move. "Name's Vess. I'm a courier." "You look like one." "I am one. I've got a crate aboard my ship that was misdirected to me. Ashline freight. It was meant for someone else's hull and the routing went sideways, and now the Ashline wants it back and they want it back from me, because I'm the only one who has it." I keep wiping the same spot. "And you're a long way from your jurisdiction." "I'm a long way from anywhere. I've been running for two days." "The Outpost is neutral ground," I say. "That's my rule. No running inside these walls, no hunting, no company business. I made it because I've seen what happens when people forget it." "I know that." She says it quietly, the way you'd say *I know you're right* to someone you're about to ask to be wrong. "I need three days. My contact comes Thursday. If I can sit still until then, I'm fine." "Sit still." "Sit still. Hide the crate. Don't report me." I look at her braids, loose and greasy with fear. "You did your homework on me." "You're the kind who can't say no. The whole belt knows it. Nets the bartender will hand you her last ration of anything, and then feel guilty about it." "Then you've found the right bar for the wrong reasons." "I've found the only bar for a while. The others turned me away in ten minutes." She pushes the glass back toward me. "I'm not asking you to like me." "What's in the crate?" "Sealed. I've got a key that opens the lid, not the truth. Ashline doesn't label their freight unless it's something they're proud of." I think about Dex at the dock window, who hears every chime and reports every company ship to whoever pays him. I think about the rule I made, and how much of my peace is stitched to it. "Company ships dock here too," I say. "Dex will hear the gate chime before I do." "Then don't let him." "That's a big ask for a double." "I've got ore credits. Vega whisky money." "I don't want your money. I want my bar." Maro leans in from his stool. "You got company trouble at the gate?" "Just a customer with a heavy drink," I say. "Maro, if anyone asks, she's mine. A cousin. Visiting." He studies Vess, then nods once, slow, and goes back to his slag. That's the thing about this place. People will take your word for a cousin. Vess exhales, and two of her braids start to re-knot themselves, slowly, the way a person might roll their shoulders. "Three days," she says. "You'll be the first person in two days who's offered me anything." I wipe the same spot. It's been clean for an hour. I keep at it anyway, because it gives my hands something to do while I decide whether my flaw is a talent or a liability, which, depending on the evening, it's both. "Sit tight," I say. "Don't move. Don't talk. And if you owe me anything after this, it's a lot." "I'll owe you whatever." The gate chime sounds, soft, the way it does when the request comes from a ship that doesn't want to be refused. Dex's voice comes through the dock window: "Nets. Ashline courier requesting clearance. Says they're carrying something that can't wait." Vess goes very still, braids hanging loose again. She looks at the door, then at me, then at her half-finished double. I look at the rag in my hand. "Hold your drink," I say, and go to answer the chime.

+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The heat in New Orleans doesn't hit you. It arrives in layers, like the city is slowly closing its hands around you. I've been walking since they dumped me at the corner of Bourbon and Decatur with a suitcase of clothes that smelled like diesel and a guy's last words: *You're too old for this, kid. Go find your own problems.* Fair enough. I have plenty. The strap of my backpack keeps sliding off my left shoulder, and every time I hitch it back up, I can feel the heat on the back of my neck where the sun finds me. I keep thinking about the thirty minutes it took to plan the escape last night. Thirty minutes to decide I was leaving a life, and now I've been walking for hours and I still don't know where I'm going. My phone died at midnight. Mom and Dad's numbers are still in it, and that's the problem. I could call them and say *I'm in New Orleans and I'm fine*, and they'd say *get on a bus* or worse, they'd say nothing at all, which is what they've said for two days. *Concerning behavioural patterns*, the counsellor called it on the phone to Mom, like I was a weather system. I'm not a pattern. I'm a person who told the truth in a kitchen and watched everyone in it turn away from me. There's a bus stop on Decatur with a bench that's been wet since Tuesday, maybe. A man in a stained polo shirt sits down next to me and waits the way people wait when they're deciding if you're worth it. "You heading somewhere, son?" "Girl," I say, which is true, and which costs me nothing here. "Where you from?" "Somewhere that doesn't have a river this big." He smiles like I've told a joke. "I got a friend who needs a hand. Easy money. You look like you could use easy money." I've been reading the news in my head for sixteen years. I know the shape of this sentence. I stand up, adjust the strap, and keep walking, and I don't look back at him, and I notice that my hands are shaking, which I hate, because I'm trying so hard not to be a kid anymore. By four o'clock I've found the thing that runaways apparently all know: the laundromats. It's called Clean Wave, on a street that smells like the river and something frying. The dryers are stacked like a hotel, and the air inside is so hot it has texture. I have four dollars and some change and a bag of clothes that need to look like they belong to a person who lives somewhere. There's a girl at the folding table near the counter, older than me, maybe eighteen, folding other people's laundry with the mechanical patience of a factory worker. She's got a braid down her back and a phone she keeps turning over in her hands without looking at it. "You got quarters?" she asks. I count out what I have. She drops them in a coffee can. "First load's free if you fold while it spins." So I fold. I learn her rhythm, which is fast and exact, and I learn that she doesn't ask where I'm from, which is the kindest thing anyone has done for me in two days. "New here?" she says finally. "Two hours." "Two hours and you're already in the right spot. You got a name?" "Taylor." "Dee. You sleep around here or you got a couch?" The strap slips off my shoulder. I fix it. "No couch." "Then you're doing this wrong. Couches are for people who have somewhere to go." She keeps folding. "I got a spot. It's not a lot. It's a back room of this place, there's a cot, and the owner thinks I'm his cousin. He's not wrong about the face." I wait for the catch. I've had forty-eight hours to learn that every kindness in my family comes with a clause. "You don't ask me anything about you," Dee says. "You don't post anywhere, you don't tell anyone where you're sleeping, and you don't owe me anything. You fold laundry when it's full. That's the whole deal." "Okay." "There's one more rule." She finally looks at me, and her eyes are tired in a way that has nothing to do with sleep. "There's a guy who works the docks near the river. He talks to kids who look like they're new. He asks where they're staying, who they're with. If he asks you, you say you're visiting a cousin in the Ninth Ward and you're leaving tomorrow. You understand?" "Okay." "Good. You're smarter than you look." I want to ask her a hundred things. Why she's folding laundry for strangers at six in the evening. Why she keeps turning that phone over like it's a talisman. Where she's running from, if she's running at all, because she has the settled look of someone who's been running so long she's forgotten the starting line. Instead I say, "Thanks." "Don't thank me. Thank the quarters." The dryer finishes. The owner, a man with a beard like a mop, waves me toward the back room without a word, which is either kindness or indifference, and I'm learning that in this city they might be the same thing. The cot is thin. The window faces a brick wall. Somewhere outside, a trumpet is practicing the same four notes over and over, patient as rain. Dee leaves me a bottle of water and a note on the pillow: *Don't sleep on your phone side.* I put my phone under the mattress anyway, because I'm sixteen and I still need my parents to find me, even though I ran away to prove I didn't. I lie there listening to the trumpet, and for the first time in two days I'm not thinking about the kitchen table. I'm thinking about tomorrow, about folding laundry, about the guy by the docks and the rules I'm supposed to follow. I pull the strap of my backpack up one more time, and this time it stays.

Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** The predicament was this: Chewy was dying, and Midas was out of beans, and the two facts were connected in the way that everything was connected now, by the simple logic of scarcity. Chewy was an animo-tronic koala from the Before,¹ stuffed with a voice box and a battery that had outlived its manufacturer, its country, and its entire understanding of what a koala was for. He sat on the edge of the mattress in the rest stop's old coffee kiosk, one ear flattened, his left arm hanging a half-inch lower than his right, repeating "Now with 30% more crunch" every ninety seconds in a voice that had gone thin as string. "Three percent," Midas said. "You've been at three percent since Tuesday." "Now with 30% more crunch," said Chewy. "We're going to the town." The town had a name once. It had been lost in the general way that names are lost, which is to say nobody had remembered to say it for long enough for anyone to learn it, and so it was simply the town, the way the sky was simply the sky, and the rain that had been coming since dawn was simply the rain. A battery is a promise made by a chemist to a future the chemist never met.² Midas needed one of those promises, in a size D, and he also needed beans, because Chewy was the only thing in the world that talked to him that didn't talk to him like he was a dog, and Chewy would not be staying at three percent. They left through the side of the kiosk where the vending machine still held a coin that Midas had been trying to reach for eleven years. The bridge over the river was gone, taken by a storm or a decision, and the detour was a field of feral wheat that stood to the shoulders and moved like a crowd deciding something. Chewy's slogans slowed as they walked, which was how you knew he was getting worse: the desperate ones come slower. The town's supermarket had doors that were fused, so they went in through a window that had been a window and then a hole and then a suggestion. Inside, the shelves stood like a picket fence with no fence, and Midas walked the aisles with the methodical grief of a man who knew what he wanted and what he would find. "Where's the beef?" said Chewy, cheerfully. "Exactly," said Midas. He found a drawer of batteries in the electronics aisle, which was a mercy, and then he found they were all AA, which was not a mercy, which was a disappointment with a smaller body. He was turning them over in his palm, thinking about what could be jury-rigged, when Chewy, in a fit of low-battery urgency, said "Ask your doctor about..." The dogs came out of the back room like a sentence finishing itself. There were four of them, grey and lean, and they had learned in the Before that voices meant something, and they were not certain what, and Midas was the nearest voice. He ran. Running is a skill that the After does not teach well, because the After is mostly about not running, and his ankle found a shopping trolley's wheel at exactly the angle of a disagreement, and he was on the ground with the dogs' interest cooling to a professional curiosity, because they had decided he was a man, and men were not interesting. He got up. He lost his pack. He retrieved the one tin of beans from the mud, which was soaked but intact, which was a victory with a damp smell. It was then that he noticed the trolley, and then that the trolley was on a slope, and then that the slope was long. He loaded Chewy in, sat behind, and let go. The trolley did what trolleys do when they are given permission: it went. Down the slope, past the rusted cars that had become furniture for birds, gathering speed with the smug momentum of something that had never once been asked to carry a koala. At the bottom it struck a bumper at a speed that was, honestly, embarrassing, and Chewy's left arm detached and rolled away into a hedge, while Midas's head met the bumper's other side with a thud that he would describe later as "structural." So the return was accomplished in multiple ways. First they walked, which was the plan. Then the trolley carried them, which was not the plan but was faster. Then, when Chewy's arm was gone and his legs were, as it turned out, decorative, Chewy rolled the last stretch on his own momentum like a ball, and Midas followed on his bad ankle, and the rain did its best to make the whole affair a washout, and nobody objected, because it was home. The arm was reattached with a strip of wire from the car they'd crashed into, which gave Chewy a slightly crooked left side, like a painting of a koala done by someone who'd had a little. Midas jury-rigged the AA batteries with a piece of wire and a prayer to no one in particular, and Chewy's eyes came on. The voice was different. Slower. Deeper. The voice of a man who sells something and genuinely believes in it. "Great Taste," said Chewy. "Less Fat." "It's beans," said Midas. "One tin." "Now with 30% more crunch," said Chewy, and his eyes glowed a colour that, in the Before, would have meant *limited offer*, and Midas sat down on the mattress in the coffee kiosk and thought that in the After, everything was a limited offer, and that this was a good day, and that Chewy, crooked-armed and overcharged and talking nonsense, was the reason for it. "You've got mail," said Chewy. "I know," said Midas. "I've been checking." --- ¹ The Before was a time when everything worked and nobody knew it, and chewed gum was a thing that happened to people. ² Batteries, it should be noted, were not the only promises the Before made. But the batteries were the ones with the best shelf life.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical asides, and footnote humor effectively. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world viewed through Pratchett's lens of absurdist observation and gentle cynicism. The story adheres well to the prompt's structure: establishing the predicament (Chewy's dying battery and need for supplies), detailing how the mission goes sideways (dogs, trolley crash, lost arm), and returning home "worse for wear" but with some success. The 1000-word count is respected. The voice is consistently Pratchettesque throughout, with memorable turns of phrase like "disappointment with a smaller body" and "momentum of something that had never once been asked to carry a koala." The footnotes are particularly well-executed, capturing Pratchett's tendency toward philosophical tangents about mundane objects. Character-wise, Midas feels authentic as a hapless protagonist, and the relationship between him and Chewy is touching without being sentimental. The animatronic koala spouting advertising slogans is both absurd and oddly poignant. Their dynamic drives the emotional core effectively. The imagery is vivid and often striking - the feral wheat "moved like a crowd deciding something" and the shelves "stood like a picket fence with no fence." The prose maintains elegance while avoiding purple excess. However, some elements feel slightly forced. The dogs' sudden appearance and equally sudden disinterest stretches believability somewhat. The trolley sequence, while entertaining, borders on slapstick in a way that doesn't quite mesh with the more subtle humor elsewhere. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - they succeed partially (battery found, Chewy repaired) but are indeed worse for wear (injury, damaged koala, jury-rigged solutions). The final exchange about having mail is a nice touch of absurdist melancholy. The dialogue, while limited, serves its purpose well, particularly Chewy's advertising slogans which become increasingly poignant as his battery fails and then changes when jury-rigged. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door gave one bright clatter and a man came in from the grey, shaking water off a hood like a dog. He was tall, dark-haired, and he moved through the shop the way a man moves when he's being followed, sideways, quick, eyes on the windows. "Can I help you?" Eleri said, not looking up from the shelf she was facing. "A book," he said. "Anything. I'm in a bit of a hurry." He settled in the corner by the poetry section, the farthest point from the front glass, and Eleri finally looked at him properly. It took her a moment, then she knew him. Declan Vane. The face from the poster on the bus stop, the one with the jaw like a chisel and the mouth that had been smiling in a hundred interviews. Outside, at the end of Chapel Street, a black car sat with its engine running and a man leaning against it, lens up. "You'll want to stay off the window," she said. "They're watching the road." "You're not going to ask for my autograph?" "I've got a queue of them in the till. Behind the bread." He laughed, and it was a good laugh, generous, aimed straight at her, and she felt the familiar small snag of it, the way his voice did things to a room. "You're funny," he said. "I like that. Most people go quiet or they go loud. You're just... practical." "Books are a practical business." "Even the poetry?" "Especially the poetry. People need to feel something for six pounds." He looked at her properly, and she saw him recalibrate, the charm shifting gears. "Right. Tell me what you've got. I'm Declan." He said it like a gift. She turned back to her shelf. "I've got a delivery of secondhand novels coming in Saturday. If you're after something specific, try the back." "I'm not after a book, love. I'm after ten minutes that aren't mine." She stopped. That was a real sentence, not a performance, and it landed somewhere inconvenient. "The kites come over the estuary at this time of year," she said, surprised by the suddenness of it. "Red kites. Big ones. They circle the church roof and you can see their shadows across the field." He turned from the poetry to the window, then back to her, hood still up. "Birdwatching?" "Most afternoons. From the back step." She tapped the field guide that lived on the counter, spine cracked, pages soft as cloth. "And in the bay, if the light's right, dolphins. Cardigan Bay's full of them." "I do it too," he said. And then, quieter, as if he hadn't meant to: "I do it in my trailer, behind the studios. Secondhand binoculars, because if you're seen with nice ones, you're seen." "That's a smart trick." "I've got about eleven tricks. They're all about not being seen." He ran a hand through his hair, a move, she knew, a move designed to be watched, but it looked almost tired. "Everyone wants a piece of me. Photographs, opinions, a look on my face for the papers. It's a lot, being a piece of everyone." "You'd think you'd like the attention." "I do like it. That's the trouble. I'm very good at liking it." She almost smiled, and caught herself, and instead pulled a box of secondhand paperbacks from the shelf and started shuffling through it. "The swifts are worth catching while they're here," she said. "They leave in September. They nest on the church, you can hear them at dusk, like a whole crowd of people arguing." "Like an audience." "Like a crowd that doesn't know your name." He went still for a moment. Then he laughed again, but smaller, and he sat down on the stool by the counter without asking. "You're not going to take a photo," he said. "You're not going to tell anyone I'm here." "I don't talk about my customers." "Declan Vane," he said, testing it out. "You know who I am. You could be famous by tomorrow. 'Bookshop girl turns away movie star.'" "Bookshop girl," she repeated. "That's not a thing anyone would say." "It would. It's the kind of thing that gets around." "Then it's not the kind of thing that gets said." He looked at her for a long moment, and she watched his face do something she hadn't seen on the posters, a little wounded, a little honest, the way a dog looks when it's been told off. "I'm sorry," he said. "I do it because it works. It's the only thing I'm good at, apparently. Being liked." "It's not that I don't like you," she said, and then shut up, having said more than planned. She picked up the field guide and, without deciding to, slid it across the counter toward him. "The swifts. Page forty-one. If you're going to watch them, watch properly." He took the book, and their fingers touched on the cracked spine, and neither of them moved away from it quickly enough. "Properly," he repeated. "You've got a way of making a bird guide sound like a dare." "I'm Welsh. We're all like that." The black car at the end of the street put on its lights and moved off, and he was on his feet before she could stop him. He pulled on his hood, paid for nothing, tipped nothing, just stood in the doorway with the bell clattering behind him. "The estuary," he said. "The kites at dusk. You said." "The estuary." "Saturday?" "The shop's open Saturdays. The kites don't care who's watching." He smiled, and this time it was aimed at nothing, at no one, and it looked like relief. "Saturday, then. I'll bring the binoculars. The secondhand ones." "Bring your own," she said, and turned back to her shelf, and shelved the same book three times before she caught herself. Outside, the grey light was going, and over the church roof, high and slow and enormous, a red kite turned its wings in the wind. She watched it until it was gone. Then she picked up the field guide from the counter, where he'd left it, held it for a moment, and put it back in its place, a little further out than it had been.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Declan's performative charm gradually giving way to vulnerability, and Eleri's dry, practical Welsh directness that masks her own attraction. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes: advancing the plot, revealing character, and building romantic tension. The Welsh setting is well-established through specific details like Chapel Street, the estuary, and Eleri's matter-of-fact reference to being Welsh. The author skillfully uses the bookstore environment and local wildlife (kites, swifts, dolphins) as both setting details and metaphorical elements that connect the characters. Character development is particularly strong. Declan is portrayed as genuinely charming but needy, with his admission "I do it because it works. It's the only thing I'm good at, apparently. Being liked" revealing the fragile ego beneath the surface. Eleri's immunity to his charm is believable - she's not rude, just unimpressed, which makes her eventual softening feel earned rather than contrived. The romantic chemistry builds naturally through their conversation about birdwatching, creating an unexpected point of connection. The moment when their fingers touch over the field guide is well-timed and not overwrought. The ending strikes an appropriate note - hopeful but not overly optimistic, with both characters maintaining their essential natures while showing subtle change. The prose is generally elegant with strong imagery, particularly the descriptions of the kites and the atmospheric details of the Welsh town. Some phrases like "jaw like a chisel" verge on cliché, but overall the writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The pacing works well, moving from the initial tension of his escape from paparazzi to the quieter, more intimate conversation about shared interests. The author successfully balances the "primarily dialogue" instruction with necessary descriptive passages. Minor weaknesses include some slightly predictable romantic beats and a few moments where the dialogue becomes slightly expository, but these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door swung inward on whalebone hinges and gave up its cold, and with it the smell of the underhold: rendered oil, wet rope, the mineral breath of deep water. Above them, the guild floor should have carried its evening noise down the stair, the pumps, the laughter, the clatter of the counting room. Nothing carried down. The quiet came up instead, thick as tallow. The stair descended into ribs. Aya had heard the founders boast that the Morska built its headquarters inside a leviathan that came ashore forty years past, and she had taken it for the kind of story men tell over brandy. Now she understood. The ribs curved overhead like the vaulting of a drowned cathedral, blackened and oiled, whale-oil lamps hanging from baleen hooks, guttering in a draft that rose from below, from the heart-chamber, where the old gold waited. "Keep to the middle of the stair," Simeon said, careful. In his waistcoat pocket, his watch ticked, loud as a metronome in the hush. "The ward is keyed to the door below. We find the key, we open, we leave." "The ward is keyed to *her*," Katra said, and her eyes were on the landing at the bottom of the stairs, where the lamps burned brighter. The landing was empty. The guard posts empty. The iron portcullis to the heart-chamber stood open on its greased wheels. Then the Anchor spoke from behind them. "No one has opened that portcullis in eleven years. Not since the gold was laid in. I'd rather you didn't try." They turned. She stood in the archway between the ribs, and she was not the woman they had watched the city guard drag screaming into the magistrate's van at dawn. The dawn woman had been gaunt, half-starved, her hands shaking. This woman stood easy as a mast in calm water. Behind her, four men in oilcloth coats held whalebone truncheons, and at her hip hung a long brass-barreled pistol of the kind the guild's own charter forbade its members to carry. Aya's mind did arithmetic it did not want to do. *The raid. The arrest. The vacuum.* "Darya," Katra breathed. "You were in the cell." "The cell holds a dockworker named Vera, who took a purse of gold to look like me," the Anchor said. "A tidy arrangement. The magistrate was paid before sunrise, and the papers were paid to print the arrest with a likeness." She smiled, a merchant's smile, weighing. "The raid was mine. I needed to know who would come for the gold in the dark, and who among my thieves could reach into the immateria and pull." The lamps flickered. Far below, something answered the word, a low vibration felt in the teeth rather than heard. Katra's hand moved to her knife. It did not get there. The truncheons were already between them and the stair, and Katra, who had drowned twice and lived, recognized the arithmetic of bodies and stopped. "Nobody moves," the Anchor said, pleasantly. "We are not here to be rude." Simeon's watch ticked on. Aya could hear it over her own pulse, which was doing something unseemly. The Anchor came down the stairs at the pace of a woman who has never once been hurried. She stopped an arm's length from Aya, took the mask in two fingers, the way one lifts a veil, and drew it off. "Ah. The girl with the pale eyes and the aristocrat's chin. Aya of the Vessel family, I believe. Your mother, then. I read the hanging notice. Immateria magick, it said. A fine thing to be born to, and a fine thing to be hanged for." *She knows.* The thought arrived late and cold. Aya had been careful, the masked prodigy of the Morska, careful that the immateria never touched her own face, that her society self and her guild self stayed as separate as oil and water. But her mother's gift ran in her blood, and blood, it turned out, was a poor secret-keeper. "You were arrested at dawn," Aya said. Her voice came out level, which surprised her. "The papers will say you're in the deep cells." "The papers say what I pay them to say. They'll say you were with me when the guard came. That is the part you should be thinking about, girl. Not me." The Anchor's eyes tracked the shape of her face like a ledger. "Your father. The Vessel name. The drawing rooms. The magistrates' wives who invite you to dinner. All of it, in next week's edition, with your mother's crime attached to your face like a brand." Aya felt the floor of her composure tilt. *Father. The drawing rooms.* She had come down these stairs to steal the guild's crown and leave aristocracy behind forever. Instead she stood with her mask in a stranger's hand, and the stranger owned the only exit. "Then kill me," Aya said. "It's simpler. And you'd be rid of the immateria question entirely." "I might. I've killed better thieves than you. But consider what I have in my belly downstairs." She gestured, and Aya looked, and there it was, in the whale's heart-chamber, ringed by lamps that burned blue-white: the gold. The Sun Stag. Scythian, ancient, wrought in the animal style, its antlers branching into a hundred small heads. It was not beautiful the way Aya had imagined. It was terrible. It looked like it was looking at her. "Eleven years I've held the key," the Anchor said. "Eleven years of keys and wards and magicians bought from three ports, and the stag has not once moved for me. The old guild-lore says it opens for blood of the immateria. I had assumed the lore was the kind of thing men invent to frighten children." She turned back to Aya. "I am no longer assuming." Simeon found his voice at last. "The ward on the door, you said keyed to her, you mean keyed to immateria? Then madam, we're worth more to you alive than dead. Katra can dive the flooded galleries. I can read any lock in the city. And she," he pointed at Aya, "she can open the stag." "Sit down," the Anchor said to Simeon. "You're doing it well." Katra said nothing. She stood very still, and Aya could see the diver's calculation in her: the truncheons, the pistol, the four men, the stair behind them guarded by more. "Here is what I propose," the Anchor said. "You three open the stag for me tonight, and you teach me what can be taught of the immateria, and in exchange you leave this whale alive, with your names scrubbed from my books and a purse to forget the evening. Refuse, and the papers get a different story, one that begins with the word *hanged*." Aya looked at the gold stag, at its hundred little heads, and thought of her mother's rope, and of how the immateria had always felt less like a gift than a debt she'd been born owing. *Her mother was hanged for what she could do. The Anchor will use what I can do. The difference is only the rope.* "And if the stag opens," Aya said, "and it takes what it takes from me, as the lore says it does, you'll keep me anyway. You'll want to see what's left." The Anchor studied her a long moment. Then she reached into her coat, plucked Simeon's watch from his waistcoat without asking, and stopped the stem with one finger. The ticking stopped. The underhold went quiet in a way that had nothing to do with the lamps. "Nothing is taken," the Anchor said. "That is what the lore says. I intend to be the first person in eleven years to test whether it's true." She handed the silent watch back to Simeon. "Time is mine to keep, now. Come, all three of you. The stag has waited this long. It can wait for your answer."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested tone and atmosphere throughout. The author successfully creates a vivid "whalepunk" setting, using the whale skeleton as guild headquarters to great atmospheric effect. The imagery is consistently evocative without becoming overwrought - descriptions like "The quiet came up instead, thick as tallow" and "ribs curved overhead like the vaulting of a drowned cathedral" establish mood efficiently. The dialogue feels authentic to the Victorian-influenced world, with characters speaking in distinct voices. The Anchor's measured, merchant-like speech contrasts well with Aya's more direct responses and Simeon's nervous formality. The author avoids modern colloquialisms while keeping the dialogue accessible. Character motivations are well-established and believable. Aya's internal conflict between her aristocratic identity and guild aspirations creates genuine tension, and her quick pivot to negotiation when unmasked feels true to her established intelligence. The Anchor emerges as a compelling antagonist - calculating and prepared rather than simply cruel. The plot adheres closely to the requested story beats while adding creative flourishes like the fake arrest scheme and the mysterious properties of the Sun Stag artifact. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from the ominous quiet to the revelation of the trap to the final negotiation. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly dense with atmospheric description, and a few instances where character thoughts could be more deeply explored. The ending, while appropriately dark for the genre, leaves some emotional threads unresolved that could have been developed further. The piece successfully avoids common pitfalls like purple prose, weak dialogue, or unearned character transformations. The world-building feels consistent and the magical elements are integrated naturally into the Victorian-influenced setting. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bar smells like spilled beer and someone's bad idea, which is the only honest sign of a place worth entering. Spike comes in first, coat open, hands loose at his sides, and orders something he can't afford. Revy comes in third, after the rain, and takes the stool two down from him because she's the kind of woman who sits where she can see the door and the exit both. "You got a contract on Reyes," she says. Not a question. He turns his head. His real eye does the work; the prosthetic one just looks, flat and patient, like a fish that died in a window. "You do too." "Then we're either partners or corpses. I've never met a third option." "Third option's a fight I already lost." He lights a cigarette with a lighter that has a ring of rust around the base, the color of dried blood, sitting at a height that tells you it's been dropped in water more than once. "You're fast though. I saw you from the street. Two guns, two hands, no wasted motion. Two Hands, they call you." "Word travels." She orders whiskey the way she orders everything: as a demand. "You're the one they call the cowboy. Nice hat. You know what I think, cowboy? I think you're broke, hungry, and you haven't slept since the Clinton administration." He laughs, short, almost apologetic. "Huh. Close enough." They drink. The jukebox plays something slow and wrong, and the bartender watches them the way you watch two dogs circling a bone, which is accurate. Revy's crop top is soaked from the rain. The dragon on her right arm coils past her elbow, scales dark as wet slate, and she keeps her left hand near her waistband the way she keeps everything near her. "You ever do a job and find out someone else's got the same name on the same head," Spike says, "and you think, maybe we should split?" "Splitting means trusting. Trusting means getting shot in the back by a guy who smiled at me first." She takes a long pull. "I don't do feelings. I do bullets." "Fair. I don't do promises either. Whatever happens, happens." "Poetic. Your mom must've been a poet." "Dead. So was mine." He doesn't elaborate, and she doesn't push, which is its own kind of respect between their kind. The trouble arrives on foot, four men, Reyes's men, who've been watching the bar from the street and decide to collect the bounty themselves. The first one fires before he's through the door. Revy is on her feet before the shell casing hits the floor, both pistols out, both hands working like they were grown together for this. Spike moves sideways instead of forward, because his depth perception is a lie his eye tells him constantly, and he's learned to let his body answer for him. His shot takes the second man's shoulder. The third man swings a knife. Spike catches the wrist, turns it, puts his boot through the man's kneecap, and the fourth one runs out into the rain. The bar is wrecked. Bottles on the floor, a hole in the jukebox, the bartender gone to the back room with his hands up. Revy checks her magazines while she talks. "You fight like a man who's been doing this longer than he's been alive." "Been dead once," he says, sitting down on an overturned chair and eating a burger from behind the bar with the concentration of a man who knows his last meal might be tonight. "Everything since is a bonus." She looks at him for a long moment. There's something in that, some crack in the armor she recognizes because she carries the same one. She doesn't say so. She says, "Reyes is holed up at the Pico Motel. Room 12. I've been circling it for two hours." "And you didn't just go in." "Two Hands can shoot, cowboy. Two Hands can't pick a lock, and Reyes's got a deadbolt and a guard dog with teeth." "Then you came here to find a partner." "I came here to see if the bounty was worth the trouble of killing you first." She drains her glass. "It's not. So. Motel. You take the front, I take the window. Nobody talks about this later." He almost smiles. "Deal." Room 12 smells of disinfectant and old cigarettes. The guard dog is a pit bull named after a general, and it goes down to Spike's shot, which surprises nobody except the dog. Reyes himself comes out holding a shotgun and a contract on a dead man, which is, in the end, exactly the kind of paperwork Spike was hired to cancel. It takes four minutes. Revy is efficient and loud about it. Spike is efficient and quiet, which is somehow worse. After, they stand in the motel room with Reyes's body cooling on the carpet and the contract in Spike's hand, and neither of them moves toward the door. "So," Revy says. She's got blood on her arm that isn't hers, and she's looking at him with those eyes that read people like receipts. "We split the money." "You could," he says. "Or you could take it all, and I could walk, and we'd both be fine with that, which is the closest thing to love I know how to offer." She stares at him. Then she reaches out and takes the lighter from his coat pocket, tilts it, catches the motel light on the rust ring around the base. "Water," she says. "More than once." "I've been under water more times than I'd like to admit." He flicks it once, twice. The flame comes up weak and orange, and he holds it under her cigarette while she leans in, close enough that their shoulders almost touch, her breath warm on his neck, his real eye tracking her mouth and her trigger finger both. "It's not romantic. It's just where the money was." "Whatever happens, happens," she repeats, and there's no mockery in it now, just the sound of a woman testing whether the words are a door or a wall. She lights up. She holds the flame there a second longer than she needs to, and he lets her. Then she puts the lighter in her own pocket, takes the contract, and hands him back nothing. "Keep your eye," she says, which is either a threat or a promise, and in her case they're the same thing. "And cowboy? If you ever need a partner who won't sell you out, you know where to find me. If you don't need me, I'll find you anyway, and I'll charge." He laughs, real this time. "Sounds expensive." "You're broke. You can afford it." She goes out the window, the way she came in, two guns swinging easy. Spike sits on the motel bed in the rain-sound, eats the rest of the burger, and watches the street where her figure is already gone. Somewhere out there she's driving toward Reyes's payment, and he's sitting in a room that isn't his, with her lighter in her pocket and his name, probably, in her head. Whatever happens, happens.

+ Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I have sat out exactly once, and it was in the winter of 1995, on a hill outside a village I had lived in for eleven months. I was fifteen. I write this down because I keep being asked, years later, whether I believe in it, and the honest answer is that I still don't know, and that the not-knowing has stayed with me longer than the cold. Astrid had been teaching me the games since October. She was sixteen, born here, and she carried a notebook of things her grandmother had taught her before the autumn the old woman died. We had done the card game for secrets, which worked, or seemed to, on our classmate Jonas, whose hidden crush we uncovered within a week and confirmed at a party. We had done the doll game for influence, which Astrid insisted was only about intention. By December she was saying that the real thing was útiseta, sitting out, and that everything else was a warm-up, like learning to swim in a bathtub before the lake. Her rules were specific. You went to the old mound, the kvarn, which sat in a clearing a kilometer past the church, a rounded hill of dark soil and stones that the village children had kicked footballs into since childhood. You went at night. You brought bread, rye, from Astrid's freezer, because her grandmother's recipe was the one that counted. You did not eat the bread until you knew whether you had been answered. You asked one question each, out loud, once, and you did not answer anything that answered back. We left Astrid's house at eleven, with a thermos of coffee and headlamps and mittens with the fingers split, the kind you could see through. The village was asleep. Snow lay deep and unbroken in the fields, and the pines along the road leaned over the path like they were trying to see us through. "The wind does it," Astrid said, when the trees started rustling as we walked. "It sounds like people talking. It's just needles. Farmor said the same thing, and I believed her, and then I stopped believing her." We sat on the north side of the mound, where the grass was worn to a path that no living person had walked in years, I thought. The soil was cold through my trousers. Somewhere a fox coughed, or the ice cracked, or both. Astrid ate nothing. She said her question was: what was I supposed to do with the notebook. Then she closed her eyes and did not move, and I sat with my bread in my lap, my breath going out in slow clouds, and I asked my question. It was a stupid question, in the way teenage questions are stupid. Is my mother staying? Because in Stockholm I had never had to ask. Here, in the kitchen, in the long cold evenings, my mother had become a person who answered everything except the thing I wanted to ask, and my father had become a man who worked at the mill and came home smelling of resin and did not look at either of us when he did. The pines rustled. It was a faint sound, almost like someone clearing their throat far away, or turning a page. Then it came again, closer, shaped, and I heard, or I assembled from the rustle, or I wished to hear, my mother's voice saying the sentence she had never once said out loud to us: *Jag vill hem.* I want to go home. My hands went numb in the mittens. I looked at Astrid, and Astrid's eyes were still closed, but her face had gone very still in a way that was not sleep, and when I touched her shoulder she flinched as if I had burned her. We sat until my legs stopped working, which Astrid said was a sign of its own, though of what she would not explain. Then, at the edge of the clearing, a light moved, a neighbor's window, or a headlamp, or nothing at all, and we walked home through the snow without speaking, the thermos between us, the bread still wrapped in Astrid's paper. At her front door she unwrapped it, broke it in two, and handed me a piece. "You eat if you got something," she said. "That's the rule." I ate. She ate. We stood in the dark doorway of a village that had been sleeping through all of it, chewing rye bread in the cold, and neither of us said what we had heard, and neither of us ever asked the other what she had heard either. The games stopped after that. Astrid said the notebook was finished, or that it wasn't ready, and I let her have it. But the line had been crossed in the simple way that lines get crossed, which is that we had sat on a hill where people were buried, we had asked dead things questions, and we had both decided, quietly, in the dark, that something had answered.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the delicate balance required for effective folk horror. The author successfully captures the voice of an adult reflecting on a formative teenage experience, with the framing device remaining appropriately transparent as requested. The prose is controlled and atmospheric, avoiding the purple excess that often plagues horror writing. The characterization is particularly effective. Linnea emerges as a believable displaced teenager caught between skepticism and desperate need for belonging, while Astrid is rendered with nuanced complexity—neither purely manipulative nor innocent, but rather a teenage girl wielding inherited knowledge she doesn't fully understand. The family dynamics are sketched economically but convincingly, with the mother's unhappiness serving as both emotional backdrop and supernatural echo. The ritual elements feel authentically researched and grounded in Scandinavian folk tradition. The specific details—rye bread from grandmother's recipe, sitting on the north side, the prohibition against answering back—create verisimilitude without overwhelming the narrative. The author maintains the crucial ambiguity between psychological and supernatural explanations throughout. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from mundane preparation through mounting unease to the climactic moment of potential contact. The imagery is consistently strong, particularly the personified pines and the careful attention to sensory details like cold and sound. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The dialogue, while functional, lacks distinctive voice—both girls speak in similar registers. Some moments veer toward telling rather than showing, particularly in explaining the family situation. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels slightly rushed compared to the careful buildup. The prose occasionally becomes slightly overwrought, though it generally maintains restraint. The piece succeeds in its primary goal of creating genuine unease while exploring themes of displacement, adolescent vulnerability, and the dangerous allure of forbidden knowledge. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Therapeutic Boundaries** The insurance company used the word *mandatory* twice in the letter, which told me everything I needed to know about how they felt about my career. I had been a sprinter. That was the whole of my identity, the only word I had ever needed when anyone asked what I did, and now I was lying on a vinyl treatment table in a clinic that smelled of eucalyptus and old liniment, being fixed by a man I had once shared a warm-up lane with. Dane rolled his sleeves to the elbow. Under his polo he wore compression sleeves, the faded geometric pattern in the club's old colors, and I recognized them immediately because I had watched him wear them on the morning my knee gave out. He had been in the lane next to mine. He had seen the buckling. "You're here," he said. Not a question. "The letter says mandatory." He looked down at my chart, then at me, and did the thing he always did, softened his mouth into something like a smile, then erased it. "Right. Mandatory." Four months since the graft. My quad had learned to be afraid. Every time my knee bent past ninety degrees, the muscle seized, a hard clench under the skin, as if it were trying to hold the joint together out of pure spite. Dane knew this better than I did, because he had watched the original tear happen in slow motion, had steadied me on the infield while the medic knelt over my leg, had told me with his hand on my shoulder that the graft would hold and the surgeon was good and I should not panic. I had panicked anyway. Then I had spent four months hating the word *recovery*, which the surgeon used and the insurance company used and Dane used, always with that clinical lightness, as if it were a gift being handed to me. "Let's start with what we've got," he said. He sat on the stool at the foot of the table and took my right leg. His hands were warm, which surprised me, because I had built up a fantasy of cold clinical hands, and instead he had the hands of a man who had done a thousand of these and who, I had to admit, had once carried me off a track. He moved my knee through passive flexion, sliding my heel toward my glutes with slow, even pressure. I felt the graft's tether before I felt the pain, that rubbery catch behind the joint, and then the pain itself, a hot line along the back of my thigh where the hamstrings fought the stretch. My hip rotated two degrees left on its own, a protective twist I couldn't stop, and Dane's forearm settled across my shin to hold it. "Sixty-two degrees," he said. "Last week it was fifty-eight." "I know. I felt it." He held. The stretch deepened by a fraction of a degree, and the pain sharpened into something precise, a point rather than a region. I could feel the exact border where hurt became harm, and I could feel him feeling it too, the way he had been trained to read a patient's face, and I was furious that he was good at reading me. "Tell me when it's the edge." "That's the edge." "Okay." He held two more degrees. "Good. That's the edge, not the cliff." I watched a water stain on the ceiling tile while I breathed through my nose, because he had asked me to breathe through my nose, and my breath came out wrong, too fast, and I didn't correct it. Once I caught myself looking at his jaw instead of the stain, and looked back at the stain on purpose, and both times I counted it as a small defeat. Then the quad sets. He pressed his thumb into the scar tissue above my kneecap and told me to contract, and I tried, and the muscle fired maybe a third of the way, a weak flutter under his thumb. He could see it. He had seen everything I had ever done on a track, so of course he could see the difference between a sprinter's quad and this. "Again. Squeeze like you're trying to flatten the patella into the bone." I did. His thumb stayed buried in the scar, and I felt the kneecap grind under it, and the pain was different this time, bright and local, a needle rather than a line. Somewhere behind my eyes my body was keeping score of how much of me had been left. Then he moved me prone, and I lay face-down with my head in the cradle, and he bent my knee under me and pressed my heel toward the vinyl. Prone knee extension. The quad had to work against gravity and against the graft and against the fear, all three at once. I felt the muscle engage late, stuttering, and Dane shifted his weight onto my thigh, a firm, even load, his forearm across my shin again, his body leaning over the table close enough that I could smell the soap he used, the same cheap soap, of all things, that he had used at the club showers ten years ago. "Again," he said. "Hold it at the top." My hand found the edge of the table. My fingers dug in. The quad burned in a way that was almost pleasant, almost like the old burns, the ones from two hundred meters into the wind, and for one second the ache in my knee was indistinguishable from the ache of training, and I hated him for that too, for being the one who could make me feel it. He released my ankle. "Two more. Then we're done." We did two more. Each one the contraction came a little earlier, the stutter shrinking, and I watched my own thigh on the table do something it hadn't done in four months, fire on command, hold, release, clean. "Thursday," he said, and pulled the sheet up to my waist with the brisk efficiency of a man very good at not being seen to linger. I sat up. My knee tracked true when I swung my legs off the table, no hesitation, no buckle, the joint simply doing its job like a hinge that had remembered how. I stood, and the floor was steady under me, and I wanted to say something that wasn't about the knee, something about the sleeves, or the morning on the track, or why he had kept the sleeves, but my mouth had been trained by four months of being fixed, and it only knew how to receive instructions. "Same time," I said. "Same time," he agreed. I went home hating the word *recovery* all over again, and hating, less, that my knee had held me up the whole way to the car.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional sophistication. The narrative successfully captures the complex psychology of a former athlete grappling with identity loss, resentment toward recovery, and unresolved tension with a former training partner now serving as their physiotherapist. The physical therapy sequences are anatomically precise and spatially coherent, meeting the prompt's demanding requirements. The author demonstrates clear understanding of rehabilitation techniques - passive flexion, quad sets, prone knee extension - and renders them with clinical accuracy while maintaining narrative tension. The progression from 58 to 62 degrees of flexion, the description of muscle firing patterns, and the spatial positioning during exercises all ring true. The character work is nuanced and psychologically believable. The protagonist's resentment toward recovery itself (not just the injury) creates compelling internal conflict. Their relationship with Dane is layered - professional distance overlaying personal history, attraction complicated by power dynamics and shared trauma. The protagonist's hyperawareness of small details (compression sleeves in old club colors, familiar soap scent) effectively conveys both attraction and the painful contrast between past and present selves. The prose maintains consistent first-person voice throughout, balancing clinical precision with emotional vulnerability. Sentences like "My quad had learned to be afraid" personify the injury in ways that feel authentic to someone whose body was once their primary tool. The writing avoids purple prose while still creating vivid sensory experiences. The sexual tension is handled with appropriate restraint - present but not overwhelming the therapeutic context. The attraction manifests through small observations and physical awareness rather than explicit content, which suits the professional boundary constraints. The ending strikes an appropriate note - small progress without false optimism. The protagonist's grudging acknowledgment that their knee "held me up the whole way to the car" suggests incremental healing while maintaining their established resistance to recovery rhetoric. Minor weaknesses include some repetitive phrasing around pain descriptions and a few moments where the clinical detail slightly interrupts narrative flow. The dialogue, while minimal, serves its purpose effectively. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The morning gun found me ashore at the factories, which was not where a lieutenant of Her Majesty's ship *Gorgon* ought to have been when the bells rang. I stood at the window of the coffee house on the wharf and watched the smoke of it climb over the junks, and I coughed, and the cough came up tasting of copper, and I blamed the sea air, because I had learned by now to blame the sea air for everything. Commander Hare came up the steps with his boots still wet. "You missed the gun, Merrick." "Sea air, sir. It's been with me since we came through the Strait." He looked at me the way he looked at a leaking pipe, with the patience of a man who has already decided it will need replacing. "You were ashore yesterday too. Twice in a week is a habit in my book." "Three days of it, sir, and I'll be aboard for the inspection." "See that you do." He paused. "They mentioned you in dispatches for the action off Borneo, in the *Lion*. Something has gone out of you since." "I was." "The fever country, perhaps. The change of water." He accepted it, because he was a commander and not a doctor, and because the alternative was a court-martial he had no evidence for. The copper taste sat in my throat like a coin I couldn't swallow. By noon the heat had the factories under a yellow lid. I crossed to the tea house on the second wharf where Tam kept his parlour behind the counter, and went in through the back door the way I had done forty times before. The room was low and dark, bamboo blinds doing their best against the sun, and the smell of it was burnt honey and tallow, the honest smell of the dragon at work. Tam weighed the Borneo on his little brass scale with the care of a man weighing a jewel. "Twelve dollars the ounce now, white man. Last month ten." "Ten it was." "Ten it was. Now the boats run slower and the Chinese look harder, and risk has a price like everything else." He folded the opium in waxed paper. "You are short." "I know I am short." He did not offer credit. He had seen too many white men with shaking hands and a cough that tasted of nothing but their own ruin, and he was not a charitable man. He was a man with a scale and a door. "There is a Mr. Pemberton, who trades in general goods, and who knows the customs boats' schedule. He has asked about you." I paid for what I could and went out into the noon. Pemberton's house was on the first wharf, all mahogany and silk, a merchant who made his money on the difference between what the Chinese wanted and what the treaties allowed. He took my hand in the Chinese way, which is to say he did not. "Lieutenant Merrick. I have a proposition, and I prefer to make it to a man I know by sight." "You know me by sight." "You know the patrol schedule for the bar tonight. Nine o'clock, the boats stand off at the mouth of the river." "I know the schedule says so." "And the junks out of Malacca, three of them, heavy, they will run at midnight if the water is dark. If they know the boats are elsewhere, they run at midnight. If they know the boats are where the schedule says, they wait." I let him finish. "You're asking me to sell the service's own watch." "I'm asking you to be paid for knowing." He opened a drawer and drew out silver dollars wrapped in paper, and the sound of them against the mahogany was the sound of the morning gun again, except this one was aimed at me. "Forty dollars. The schedule is worth more than that. I am generous." I counted. Forty was not enough for a week of Borneo. Forty was enough for four days if I smoked thin. I told him the boats would be at the bar at nine and that a headache would keep me ashore until evening, which was true in the way that all my excuses had become true. He pressed the paper into my coat. "The junks will thank you. The junks are not men who forget." That was the worst of it, more than the shaking, more than the copper: that I was now a man who had been thanked by smugglers, and that the thanks had a smell like burnt honey. The lamps came up along the river by six, the factories lit their windows, and I went back to Tam's parlour with the paper in my pocket pressing against my ribs like a second heart. The boy brought the pipe and the little lamp and said nothing, because the boy had learned long ago that a white man in that room was not a man at all but a mouth. I laid the Borneo on the pipe's bowl, small as a grain of rice, and watched it soften in the flame, and the cough came up again, tasting of copper, and I did not blame the sea air this time, because there was no sea in the room, and because I had stopped needing the excuse. It had done its work. The pipe was warm in my hand and the day was paid for, all of it, the gun I'd missed, the schedule I'd sold, the men who would be caught at the bar tomorrow and beaten for a job I'd stolen from them. The boy set down the lamp and stood in the doorway, patient as a dog. "For tomorrow, sir?" "Yes," I said. "Bring more."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric writing, effectively capturing the degradation of a British naval officer caught in opium addiction in 1830s Canton. The author successfully creates a convincing period voice through careful word choice and sentence structure that feels authentically Victorian without being pastiche. The characterization of Lieutenant Merrick is particularly well-executed. His internal justifications ("I blamed the sea air for everything") and the way he rationalizes his betrayals show psychological depth. The progression from missing duty to selling patrol schedules feels organic and believable, showing how addiction erodes moral boundaries incrementally. The dialogue serves multiple functions effectively - revealing character, advancing plot, and establishing the transactional nature of Merrick's relationships. Commander Hare's interaction establishes the military context and Merrick's declining reputation, while Tam's businesslike approach and Pemberton's careful proposition show how Merrick has become a commodity in Canton's underworld. The sensory details are particularly strong - the "copper taste" that recurs throughout, the "burnt honey and tallow" smell of the opium den, the sound of silver dollars against mahogany. These details ground the reader in the physical reality while serving symbolic functions. The structure follows Merrick's descent through a single day effectively, from missing morning gun to evening in the opium den. The pacing builds tension through each transaction, culminating in his final surrender to the addiction. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overly literary language that can feel slightly forced ("the yellow lid" of heat, "patient as a dog"). Some metaphors, while evocative, border on purple prose. The ending, while thematically appropriate, lacks surprise - the trajectory feels somewhat predetermined from the opening. The historical setting is convincingly rendered without excessive exposition, and the moral complexity of the situation - a decorated officer's fall, the colonial context, the web of corruption - adds depth beyond simple addiction narrative.
