+ Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The hill was doing what hills do at dawn, which is to say it was mostly still dark and getting brighter in the general direction of the sun. Sisyphus had the boulder at the foot of the hill, where it belonged, and Crow on top of it, where Crow belonged, wings folded, beak busy with a reed pen and a small inkpot that he had somehow made manageable over the centuries. "You're early," said Sisyphus. "I've been here since before you were," said Crow. "You were here before I was? That's not possible. I'm the oldest thing on this hill." "You're the biggest thing on this hill," said Crow. "That's different." "Right. Well. Mail?" Crow produced a bundle tied with string. "Five letters. One is about a husband's mouth-breathing. One is about a boss. One is about a dog. One is about a young man who has run out of things to be good at. And one," said Crow, squaring his shoulders, "is a little difficult." "Difficult in what way?" "I'll let you read that one aloud." "Very well. Start with the mouth-breathing." "From a woman in Corinth. She writes that her husband sleeps with his mouth open and it is, in her words, 'a constant reminder that he exists.'" "Tell her it is not her job to remind him he exists. Tell her to put a pillow over his face and sleep. If he wakes up feeling smothered, that is between him and the pillow. Tell her also that she has been married to him long enough to know that he will not change, and that knowing this is a kind of peace." Crow wrote. "Next." "A man in Athens. His boss says they are 'a family', and therefore he must be available on Saturdays, and he cannot work out how to say no without being ungrateful." "Tell him that families do not bill for their time. If his boss wants him on Saturdays, he should pay him for Saturdays. Family members are not paid. That is rather what makes them family. And tell him that you cannot carry everything at once. Set the heavy thing down for a minute. It will still be there. It always is." Crow wrote, and paused. "That last part is very like you." "Everything is very like me," said Sisyphus. "I'm the only thing around here." "Third letter. A woman whose neighbour keeps walking his dog on her grass." "Tell her that a fence keeps out dogs, but it also keeps out the dog's owner's apologies. She should say to the man: 'The dog is welcome on my grass. The man is less so.' Then watch what happens." "Fourth. A young man who has finished everything he was taught to finish, and now stands around wondering what comes next." "Tell him there is no list. There never was. People have been standing around wondering for centuries, and the ones who got on with it were usually the ones who started with something small and boring, like feeding the chickens. Tell him to feed some chickens." "And the difficult one?" Sisyphus took the letter and read it, and then looked at it again, and then at Crow. "A man writes that he has been seeing another man, and that his wife knows, and that he would like to know whether he should confess the extent of it, or simply keep the current arrangement and call it 'complicated.'" "Tell him that 'complicated' is a word people use when they are frightened of the simpler word, which is 'lying.' He should tell his wife the truth, all of it, once, and then stop being complicated. Tell him it will be worse for a week and better for the rest of his life." Crow wrote this down with the air of a man who had seen worse and was professionally unimpressed. It was at this point that the god of the Almost arrived.¹ He was a small god, in the way that minor deities are small, which is to say he took up very little space and very little notice. His portfolio included the moment you reach for your keys and realise you are holding them, the word that will come to you in the bath, and the bus that pulls away as you run. "An advice column," he said, landing on a rock with the dignity of a man who had once been almost famous. "From the man who cannot even push his boulder over the crest." "That is true," said Sisyphus. "I never can." "You should be suffering. There is a whole tradition of suffering. It is what you are for. You are pushing a stone up a hill and you are using the time to give people advice about their husbands." "The husband was the easy one," said Sisyphus. "The paper is also terrible," said the god. "And the ink. And your handwriting is terrible, which is forgivable, because you are pushing a stone, but the crow's handwriting is not terrible, and that is a different matter entirely." "That's all very well," said Sisyphus. "And I'm sorry the paper is cheap. The ink is better than it used to be. Crow, note that down." Crow noted it down. "Hobbies," said the god, "are for people with time." "Time," said Sisyphus, "is rather the one thing I have in abundance. It is what I have. It is, in fact, all I have. So I thought I would do something with it that didn't involve me." The god of the Almost stood there for a moment, having almost said something more. Then he left, which was, in a sense, his whole job. "Crow," said Sisyphus, "is there another one?" "There's always another one," said Crow. "That's the good news." Sisyphus began to push. The boulder went up the hill, and Crow rode along on top of it, taking dictation, and the letters kept coming, as letters do, from everywhere, asking him about everything, and he answered them all. --- ¹ The god of the Almost had once been the god of the Almost Famous, but found the portfolio too heavy and downgraded himself. He is content. He is almost always content.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive voice and style, successfully capturing his dry wit, philosophical undertones, and characteristic footnote humor. The author effectively establishes Sisyphus as a surprisingly grounded advice columnist, avoiding the obvious boulder metaphors and stoic clichés as requested. The epistolary format works well, with each advice letter feeling authentic and varied in tone - from mundane domestic complaints to more complex moral dilemmas. Sisyphus's responses are genuinely insightful and practical, showing rather than telling his wisdom through concrete, actionable advice. His suggestion about the "family" workplace dynamic and the distinction between complicated and lying are particularly well-crafted. The dialogue between Sisyphus and Crow feels natural and establishes their relationship efficiently. Crow's dry professionalism ("professionally unimpressed") and their casual banter about age and existence captures Pratchett's ability to find humor in the mundane aspects of extraordinary situations. The introduction of the god of the Almost provides effective conflict and commentary on Sisyphus's unconventional approach to his punishment. The god's complaint about suffering traditions is both funny and thematically relevant, while the footnote about his career downgrade is pure Pratchett. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The opening description, while atmospheric, feels slightly forced in its Pratchett imitation ("doing what hills do at dawn"). Some transitions between advice letters feel abrupt, and the piece could benefit from more varied pacing. The ending, while thematically appropriate, lacks the punch or memorable final image that would elevate it from good to exceptional. The writing successfully avoids being overwrought or purple, maintaining the understated humor requested. The characterization of Sisyphus as genuinely enjoying his new role comes through clearly without heavy-handed exposition. The piece shows good understanding of the prompt's requirements, particularly in making Sisyphus surprisingly natural at advice-giving rather than playing up fish-out-of-water comedy. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The guitar cut through the arcade's noise like it had personal grievances with the noise. Saki stopped between two stacked shopfronts, still staring at the price sticker on a Juno-60 in the window, and turned toward the entrance of the arcade where a girl with a battered electric guitar was finishing a set. The last notes were the Gurren Lagann theme, played so fast the melody nearly dissolved into pure energy. Coins clattered into the open case. "That's it for tonight," the girl said, unplugging with the casual efficiency of someone who'd done it a hundred times. "Thank you for the change." Most people drifted back toward the arcade. Saki didn't move. She wasn't sure she was going to move. "Oi." The girl looked at her. "You're the only one who stayed for the whole thing. Either you love it, or you're lost." "It's... Yamato Nadeshiko Rock Revolution. From Gurren Lagann." "...You know the song?" "I, yeah. The intro's in D minor and the chorus jumps to B major. That's why it feels like it's climbing." The girl tilted her head, studying her the way you'd study a vending machine that had just given you the wrong drink. "Okay. That's not lost. That's, what's that, a professor?" "Sorry?" "Nothing. What do you play?" "Synth." "Oh, cool. What do you, is that a thing you can play loud?" "You can." "Okay." The girl slung her guitar case over one shoulder, and the grin turned curious instead of teasing. "I've been meaning to ask someone. There was a girl at a festival with a whole rack of boxes, just pressing things, and it sounded like a spaceship dying. Was that synths?" "Probably. What did it sound like?" "I don't know. Like the sea, but the sea is angry and also a little bit scared." Saki almost laughed. Almost. "That's probably a granular synth." "Say that again. Slower. Like I'm smart." "It's a technique where you chop a sound into tiny pieces and reassemble them. You take one recording and make it into anything. Rain. Glass. A voice, if you squish it enough." The girl considered this. "I could do that with my guitar. I could chop up my own playing." "You could try." "I feel like that's advice from someone who knows what they're talking about." She started walking toward the exit, then turned back. "There's a kaitenzushi two blocks over. My treat, if you tell me what I'm doing wrong with my playing." "You're not doing anything wrong." "Then it's a free dinner." Saki looked at the arcade, at the Juno-60 behind her, at the safe familiar streets she'd planned to walk back down. Then she followed. The restaurant was small and loud with the hum of the conveyor motors. They sat across from each other at the counter, and the belt brought them tuna, salmon, and a plate with a name Saki didn't recognize, which she ate anyway because refusing food felt rude and she was hungry. "So," the girl said, popping a piece of salmon in. "You said synth. Do you own one?" "A Minilogue. And a broken Juno I'm slowly fixing." "You fix your own synths?" "I fix my own synths." "Okay, that's the coolest thing anyone's said to me this week." The girl leaned back. "My name's Yuki, by the way. I'm nineteen. I busk because it's the only job that lets me play all day." "Saki. Sixteen." "Sixteen and fixing Junos. I'm jealous, honestly." They talked about gear, about the used-synth shops in Den Den Town, about whether Yuki should get a proper amp instead of the small one she dragged everywhere. Yuki listened with her chin on her hand and asked real questions, and Saki found herself talking longer than she usually did, which was strange, because she'd planned on being quiet. "What made you pick the Gurren theme?" Saki asked. "It's... obvious." "Is it? I picked it because it's the song that makes people look up from their phones. It's a crowd song." Yuki shrugged. "But I've got a guilty one too. I found a list of anime soundtracks that are 'underrated,' and one of them wrecked me." "Which one?" "Texhnolyze. I don't even know why I liked it. There's no melody you can hum. It's just... dark. But I listened to it twice in one sitting and then I was sad for a week." Saki stopped chewing. "You listened to it twice in one sitting?" "Yeah? It's only like an hour." "The score is over three hours long." Yuki blinked. "Okay. That's a lot of sad." "It's Yuki Kajiura's work. It's built on one motif, this short phrase that keeps coming back, but every time it comes back it's a little more broken. Chopped up. It's like that granular thing I told you about, except done by a human with a feeling." "Wait." Yuki put her chopsticks down. "You know it?" "I've been transcribing it. The Lacuna theme. I've been trying to build it on my Minilogue for months." "And?" "And I haven't played it for anyone yet." Yuki studied her for a second, and for once the grin was off her face. "You should. When you're done." "It's not finished." "Play it unfinished. That's what I do out there, with or without a crowd." She slid a plate of salmon across the belt toward Saki, who caught it before it could pass. "I busk Thursday and Saturday. Outside the arcade where you found me. If you're ever around Den Den Town, come hear something harder. I've been meaning to try something slower. Something with, what was it, choppy sounds." Saki looked down at the plate. "Maybe." "Maybe's good," Yuki said. "You said maybe." That was it, no phone numbers, no promises, just the belt humming around them and the two of them eating sushi in the warm evening, and Saki thinking, very quietly, that she would come back on Thursday.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character development within the slice-of-life genre. The author successfully captures two distinct voices through dialogue - Saki's hesitant, knowledge-heavy speech patterns contrast effectively with Yuki's casual, confident tone. The setting of Den Den Town feels authentic, with specific details like the Juno-60 and kaitenzushi restaurant grounding the scene in place. The character dynamics work well, showing genuine chemistry between the introverted synth enthusiast and the outgoing busker. Their conversation flows naturally from music theory to personal connection, avoiding forced exposition. The author handles the shy character's gradual opening up believably, particularly in moments like "Saki found herself talking longer than she usually did, which was strange." The prose style is generally clean and effective, with some particularly strong moments like "The guitar cut through the arcade's noise like it had personal grievances with the noise." However, there are occasional awkward constructions and the piece sometimes lacks the lyrical quality that would elevate it from competent to exceptional. The emotional arc feels earned - the connection between the characters develops organically through shared musical interests rather than forced circumstances. The ending strikes an appropriate note of possibility without overselling the relationship's development. Some weaknesses include moments where the dialogue becomes slightly expository (explaining synth techniques) and occasional unclear phrasing. The piece also plays things relatively safe within genre conventions, though it executes them well. The character of Saki could have been pushed further in terms of her internal experience and growth. The technical music knowledge adds authenticity without overwhelming non-expert readers, and the cultural details feel researched rather than superficial. Overall, this is solid, engaging writing that fulfills its brief effectively while showing genuine craft in character voice and relationship development. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**The Rewind** You know you're in trouble when your smart watch starts showing things that aren't on any app. It came in a box that was warm, like something had been sleeping inside it. Your mom bought it from a clearance bin at the electronics store, and the clerk wouldn't look at you when she rang it up. She said, "It's on sale for a reason," and then she wouldn't say what reason. The watch had a black band, a round face, and one button on the side that did nothing useful. You pressed it anyway, just to see. Time hiccuped. The milk carton you'd dropped on the kitchen floor was back in your hand, dry. Your mom was still talking, mid-sentence, about something she'd said thirty seconds ago. You blinked. She blinked. Neither of you noticed. You pressed it again after class, when you gave the wrong answer in front of the whole room. The world sucked inward like a vacuum cleaner, colors smearing, and suddenly you were sitting down with your hand raised, the right answer still inside your head. You pressed it a third time when you and Dana got into it over the game controller. Each press, the same pull, like being dragged by the hair through a drain. Each time, back to just before the mistake. The watch face flickered sometimes. Numbers you couldn't read, like 00:00:00, or 88:88:88, gone before you could study them. You figured it was a glitch. Then the growing pains started. Not the normal kind. Your shoes went tight in a week. Your mom marked your height on the doorframe every Sunday and started saying things like, "You're growing like a weed, sweetheart." Your voice cracked on the stairs. Your knuckles looked like your dad's. The watch band, which had fit snug, now slid around your wrist. Mr. Okafor said, "You're not in my class anymore, are you? You're in seventh." Dana said, "Dude, when did you get so tall?" You told them all it was puberty. It was the only thing you knew. Then came Tuesday. Your mom crossed Maple and Fifth at 8:15, and a big rig ran the light. The phone call from your dad was flat and small, like it had been shrunk down to fit in his mouth. You sat on the bathroom floor with the watch in your hands and pressed the button so hard your thumb ached. You held it down. You screamed inside your own head, *not this, not this, take it back, take it back.* The pull was violent this time. You woke at the kitchen table, and your mom was humming while she made eggs. You were also wrong. Your body felt like a coat that had been stretched on a too-big frame. You were seventeen in a twelve-year-old's house. "Sweetheart," your mom said, "you look so old. Are you sick?" Dad asked you to help change his tire. Mr. Okafor asked you to tutor the sixth graders. Your mom started asking you to hold the house together. You were happy for about a day. Then the news came at lunch. Maple and Fifth. Big rig. A girl walking home with a red backpack. Dana. You sat in the cafeteria and did the math, and the math was simple and it was awful. The truck hadn't missed your mom by luck. The truck kept its appointment. You had just moved the target. People treated you differently after that. Dana's mom wouldn't meet your eyes. Your own mom held your hand at the funeral and whispered, "It's like you grew up overnight." The countdown flickered more often now. 00:00:00. 00:00:01. You finally understood it wasn't counting down to anything. It was counting what you had left. Or counting you down. One more press. You knew it the way you knew your own name. One more press and everything went back: the eggs, the tire, the funeral, the tall body. Mom back where she belonged. Dana alive, arguing about whose turn it was to take the controller. And you, twelve, small, with a watch that fit. You pressed it. The world spun. You felt the years peel off, felt your knees knock together, felt your voice go high and thin. You woke at the kitchen table. Tuesday. 7:40. Eggs. Mom humming. Your wrist was small again. Your hands were small. No watch. Somewhere across town, you knew, a girl with a red backpack was alive and happy and unaware that she had ever been dead. You said nothing. You ate your eggs. At 7:58 you ran to the door. "Mom, don't go! Don't leave the house today, please!" She looked at you like you'd lost your mind. "What do you mean, honey? I've got to be at work by eight-thirty." She kissed your head. The door closed. You stood on the porch and watched her taillights turn onto Maple. The watch was gone, but you could still feel the button under your skin, a phantom itch. 8:12. You ran. You made it to the corner of Maple and Fifth with two minutes to spare, lungs burning, and stood in the crosswalk watching the light. Green. The intersection was empty. Then, from the east, you heard the horn of a big rig. And the light turned, and turned, and stayed red.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Goosebumps-style teen horror prompt, incorporating all required elements: the smart watch with time-rewinding abilities, physical aging consequences, changing social treatment, timeline shifts with disastrous results, and the final attempt at resolution. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The shooting gallery squatted at the bend where the boardwalk's iron railing gave way to the sea, a lean-to of plywood and neon, a shelf of tin cans behind glass, a row of little rifles no one was holding. Verna stopped just short of it and let her fingers find the note in her pocket, folded in thirds, unsigned, the address and the hour written in a hand that was careful about itself. He was already there. He sat on the bench the owner had dragged out for the old ladies, one elbow on the back of it, not touching a rifle. The new bulbs had just come on and buzzed, and his curls caught them, black as a beetle's wing, and his eyes were darker still. He looked up the way a man looks up at something he has been waiting for all day. "Verna." Not a question. "You know my name," she said. "I know your name, your address, and the fact that you work Tuesdays and Thursdays at the pawn shop on Flatbush Avenue." He smiled, and it was a pleasant smile, which made it worse. "I'm not going to frighten you. I'd like to offer you something." "I'm not frightened." "You're wearing gloves in July." "Habit." "A habit from cold work, or careful work?" She didn't answer. The cotton candy cart was passing, pink sugar steaming off the paper cone, and the smell went into her and would not leave. It brought the old thing with it, the half-formed memory. A carnival, sugar and hot grease, and her father's voice saying *watch*, and then her own small fingers doing what his had done, the pin turning, the tumblers letting go, the little gate swinging open. She had been nine, maybe ten. She could not place the year, and her mother had taught her not to ask. The last cotton candy she had tasted was the day her father went away, or the day he came back empty-handed, and she had never managed to decide which. Now this stranger's hands rested on the bench, long-fingered and still, and she saw her father's in them, and the phrase came again, *his locks*, and she pushed it down hard. "You wrote me a note that said nothing," she said. "It said everything. It said the shooting gallery, the bend of the boardwalk, when the lights come on." "And if I hadn't come?" "Then you'd be home now, wearing gloves in the dark, thinking about it." Something in her moved. She had promised herself she was coming to tell him to stop writing, and she hated that he was right about the thinking. "His locks," she said, and stopped herself. He waited. That was the worst of him, the waiting. "What?" she said. "Nothing." "You said something." "I said the candy's gone soft. I was going to say I don't eat cotton candy." "Neither do I." "Then why does the smell keep bringing you back here?" She looked at him properly for the first time. Younger than the note had suggested, maybe twenty-five, with hair that looked expensive and eyes that had watched a great deal. "What do you want from me?" she asked. "There's a safe that needs opening. Private place. A man who deserves it." "A man who deserves what?" "Whatever's in the safe. I don't need to know." "You're a thief." "I'm a man with a job that needs a woman with your hands." He said it gently, the way you'd say *you have lovely teeth*. "I've looked at safes for eleven years. I've never once needed a pick that worked first try. Yours would." "My father was a locksmith." "Your father was a locksmith who did something in Chicago and never came back." He said it without heat, which was its own kind of heat. "I've read about him too. I'd like to think you're better than he was." The boardwalk behind them was thinning. The Cyclone shrieked somewhere past the midway, and a calliope wheezed out a tune that had no business being cheerful. "Why me?" she said. "There are women in this city who pick locks for a living and never once get written to by a stranger." "Because you're careful. And because you're lonely. And because I've watched you at that pawn shop for two months, Verna, and you open the back safe every night at eleven with a pick made from a paperclip, and you do it better than any man I know." There it was. The thing she had told herself she was coming to deny. She stood very still while the sea filled the silence. "Say no," she said, "and I'll say no." "Say no and I'll go home and write again." "Say yes and I want to know what's in it for me." "That's the right question." He stood up and brushed the bench with his sleeve, and up close his eyes were not dark at all but brown, ordinary, almost kind. "Money, for the first job. A way out of pawn shop nights, for the rest of them. And a man who would never write you a note like that again, because you'd know his name." "And if I say yes and you're wrong about me?" "Then I'll be a fool, and fools are cheap in July." The gallery owner came out to rack the cans, calling the last light. "I need to think," she said. "You have until the lights go out." He tipped his head, not his hat, and turned toward the Wonder Wheel, whose spokes were turning slow against the sky, each car lit like a small burning room. Verna stood at the shooting gallery with the tin cans and the empty rifles and the smell of sugar and salt, and thought about her father's hands, and the gate swinging open, and eleven years of a man who had never once needed her kind of hands. She bought a stick of cotton candy from the passing cart. It tasted like nothing she could place, which was its own comfort. Then she walked after him.

+ Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The coffee at the lodge had always tasted like it was brewed by a man who didn't believe in coffee. JT drank it anyway, standing at the kitchen counter with his back to the fire, listening to his father's boots on the porch boards outside. "Morning," his father said. "Morning." The buck had been three days now, and his father had mentioned it once, at dinner, in passing, the way you mention weather. "Good animal out there," he'd said. "Big one. Quiet." Nobody had asked anything, because nobody had seen anything, as far as JT knew. He'd seen something. He kept it the way you keep a broken bone, inside, where it hurts but doesn't show. Mike came in with a bag from the village store, a four-mile drive on a road that went no further than the store. "They got a new clerk," Mike said. "Kid. Couldn't tell you if he was selling us coffee or cigarettes." "Put them on the table." JT went outside to get the rifles out of the truck and felt the woods the way you feel a hand on your shoulder. He could not have said what he felt, and that was the problem. The eyes of the buck. He tried to remember the eyes. He got dark, and then he got nothing, and then he got the memory of dark, which was not the same thing. His father was already out by the woodpile, axe resting against his hip, watching the clearing through the birch. "Dad," JT said. "What are we shooting at tomorrow?" His father turned. His face was fine. That was the worst part. His face was fine and kind and a little too still. "Whatever's out there," he said. "Caribou's been good to us this year." Gus had driven them up in September and talked the whole way, the way Gus always talked, about his mother's garden, about a moose he'd once mistaken for a very large dog, about the price of moose meat in town, which was down again. This year he'd talked for the first hour and then stopped, and he'd stopped again at the lodge, and again at breakfast. He sat with his hat in his lap and looked at the stove. JT found him in the barn that afternoon, sitting on a hay bale with the truck keys turning over in his palm like a coin. "Where's your rifle?" JT asked. "Left it in the cab." "Since when do you not carry?" Gus looked at him. He was fifty-something, maybe sixty, with a beard like a hedgehog and hands that had held ropes his whole life. He'd guided JT's father for twenty years. He told stories for fun, that was half the job. "Since I drove out to the salt licks Tuesday," Gus said. "What about the salt licks?" "Sixty head of them. Standing." JT waited. "Standing still. In the clearing by the lodge. All day. Caribou don't stand still, JT. You know that. They're runners. They run and they run, and when they stop it's because they're dead." "Maybe they were resting." "Sixty animals resting in a circle." Gus turned the keys over once more. "All facing the same direction. Facing your clearing. Facing where you three stood with the rifles down." JT felt the cold find a place in his stomach and stay there. "Maybe they were curious." "Curious." Gus said it the way a man says the name of a disease he's heard about. "My grandad used to say the moon does something up here in October. Says the herd goes quiet before the full moon because something comes out to count them. He was a fool who told stories. He was also a man who never hunted after the full moon, not once in eighty years." "What do you want us to do?" "Leave. Two nights out from full. I'm not taking you out tomorrow. The truck's leaving whether you're in it or not, and I'd rather you were in it." JT looked at the barn door, at the light coming through it, grey at the edges. "Will you tell my dad?" "I told him. He said the animals were at peace this year. He said I was being soft." Gus looked at JT again, and for the first time the guide looked afraid, afraid of the man he'd guided for twenty years. "He asked me if I was sure. Like it was a question about weather." At dinner JT tried it anyway. He put down his fork. "Dad," he said. "Gus says the herd's been standing in the clearing all week." His father chewed. Swallowed. Wiped his mouth with a napkin like a man who had all the time in the world. "Gus is a good man," his father said. "He tells good stories. You ever notice how he always knows the price of everything in town?" Mike, from across the table: "JT, you been hiding behind bushes all week." "I had a bootlace." "You had a bootlace." Mike looked at their father. "Dad, remember the buck? The one you almost petted?" Their father set his napkin down neatly. "That was a big buck, Mike. You can tell a lot about an animal by how still it stands." JT looked at his plate. Beans. Gravy. The gravy was doing something slow in the middle of it, a little boil, like it was thinking too. "Okay," JT said. "Okay." That night the moon came up fat and early, nearly full, with two nights left in it. JT lay in the top bunk of the room he and Mike shared, listening to the lodge settle. No cell signal. No radio but the battery one Mike kept for the truck, which he'd forgotten to charge. Around two he heard his father's boots on the porch boards. JT got up, pulled a parka over his sleeping bag, and went out barefoot onto the frozen steps. There his father stood, rifle slung across his back, collar up, looking at the clearing the way you look at a house you're about to move into. "Dad," JT said. "It's two in the morning." "Can't sleep," his father said. "Thought I'd walk." JT followed him. He followed because he was twenty-three and his father was fifty-six and had never once in his life walked into the woods at night without a reason, and the reason was what JT needed to see. They got to the edge of the clearing and the moonlight came down through the birch in long pale sheets, and JT saw them. The herd. Maybe sixty, maybe more, standing in the open space where the buck had stood, arranged in a loose circle, and not one of them moving, and all of them facing the same direction. Facing JT's father, who stood in the middle of the circle with his rifle still slung and his hand raised, open-palmed, the way you greet somebody at a gate. And from the trees, the sound of hooves, coming in from everywhere at once, more of them, walking, filling the edge of the circle, and his father's voice, soft, carrying on the still air: "There you are," his father said. "You've been so quiet." JT's hand found the birch line behind him and held on. He thought about the truck keys in Gus's pocket, four miles south. He thought about the full moon, two nights out. He thought about how his father had always said what he meant, and how he'd never in his life called an animal by its name, and how the herd had stopped, all of them, at once, the way a room goes quiet when somebody's gone inside. He did not follow his father into the clearing. He stood in the birch line with the cold coming through his boots and watched the circle get smaller, and he counted the animals the way Gus's grandad said something came out to count them, and he counted to sixty, and then he counted again, and got sixty-one.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Stephen King-inspired surreal horror style requested, maintaining the established voice and atmosphere while advancing the narrative effectively. The writing captures JT's perspective as an unreliable narrator caught between doubt and growing dread, successfully building tension toward a genuinely unsettling climax. The characterization is particularly strong. JT's internal conflict feels authentic - his reluctance to voice his concerns, his protective instincts toward his father, and his growing isolation are all believable. The father's transformation is subtle and disturbing, shown through small details like his "too still" face and uncharacteristic nighttime behavior. Gus serves as an effective exposition vehicle while maintaining his own distinct voice and motivations. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, building tension, and providing backstory without feeling forced. Gus's explanation about the salt licks and his grandfather's warnings feels organic to his character as a longtime guide. The dinner conversation effectively shows the family dynamics and the father's concerning detachment. The imagery is consistently strong throughout, from the opening coffee description to the final moonlit clearing scene. The author uses concrete, sensory details effectively - the "gravy doing something slow in the middle" is particularly evocative. The final scene with the caribou circle is genuinely haunting and well-executed. The pacing builds tension steadily, moving from JT's morning unease through Gus's warnings to the climactic nighttime encounter. The structure feels purposeful, with each scene adding layers to the mystery while deepening JT's isolation. However, there are some minor weaknesses. Occasionally the prose becomes slightly overwrought, particularly in some of the more metaphorical passages. A few transitions feel abrupt, and some of the more abstract descriptions could be clearer. The piece also relies somewhat heavily on familiar horror tropes, though it executes them well. The ending is genuinely creepy and well-earned, with the counting motif paying off effectively. The final image of JT counting "sixty-one" animals provides a perfect note of ambiguous dread that fits the surreal horror genre perfectly. # Hell is Other Demons Hell does not have a morning, exactly, but it has a shift change, and Lucifer found the shift change disagreeable in the way that all transitions are disagreeable, including the one between *off* and *on again*. He descended through the upper halls in his robe, which was black because black was the only colour that didn't have to be explained. Below him, the screaming went on at its usual volume, which the engineers had recently calibrated to *adequate*. He had once wanted it louder. Then quieter. Then, he had admitted to no one, he had wanted it to stop for an hour so he could hear whether anything else in Hell made any sound at all. Astoreth met him at the third landing. Astoreth had been promoted by mistake, and had since performed his duties with the furious competence of a man who suspected the mistake would eventually be noticed. "Morning, sir. The Greed circle's intake forms are jamming again. And Charon's on strike. Pension." "Charon has ferried the dead for six thousand years. He doesn't want a pension." "He wants it in principle, sir. He's got a solicitor now. A mortal one, who died in a meeting about it." Lucifer stamped the relevant form, red wax, the stamp he'd used since before the concept of stamps, and went on. The river below churned its grey water. The ferry was moored and empty. Somewhere a soul was being boiled for the first time, and the sound of it was like a kettle, if kettles were also, occasionally, screaming. He had a desk in the middle of the second circle, which was a practical arrangement, since the second circle was where Hell's paperwork went to be kept warm. The ledger lay open. The paperweight was a petrified scream, a gift from an earlier reign. He had not written anything in it for three days, which was unusual, because the ledger was mostly full of him. The spare room was aired. He'd aired it that morning, and the morning before, and he'd replaced the moth lamp with one that had a nicer shade. There were moths now. There were, in fact, quite a few moths, which was a small scandal, since moths required warmth, and warmth was something Hell was constitutionally incapable of providing. He ate lunch alone at the table where he'd once eaten dinners with someone, and the table was long, and the table had not been shortened, and he thought about this for a moment and then about the intake forms instead. She came through the wall at half past two, which was the way she always came, because she considered the gate a formality she'd outgrown. She wore a coat that had been good in the mortal world and was now mostly ash. The scorched leather purse hung at her hip, soft as an old glove. "Good afternoon," she said. "I've brought you a thing." She opened the purse on his desk. Inside, among the usual contents, a child's shoe, a bottle of something that had no label, a toothpick, a photograph of a dog that had died of old age and was therefore, technically, a demon now, there sat a rubber chicken. "A carnival in Lisbon," she said. "A man bought one for his daughter and she threw it at a clown. I thought you'd like it. For your desk." He put the chicken on his desk, beside the petrified scream. "Why?" "I was in the area." "You were in the area. Of Lisbon." "I have a wide area." She was not here to burn anything. She was not here to demand anything, which was the thing that frightened him slightly, because it meant she was here for the reasons that had no forms, and the reasons that had no forms were the ones that used to keep him awake. "You've got the moths back," she said, looking up at the lamp. "I've been meaning to tell you." "You've been meaning to tell me a lot of things. You've been meaning to tell me since before the moths." She closed the purse. "The kettle's been warm all day. I could smell it through the wall." He did not answer this. He poured two cups instead, because the good cup, the one with the chip in it, had been in the cupboard, and he had taken it out without remembering to, and now it was in her hands, and the tea was in it, and neither of them was going to be the one to mention the cupboard. They drank. Outside, the screaming went on, adequate. "I should tell you," she said, "that I'm not here to talk." "Good. Neither am I." She stayed anyway, for an hour, sitting in the chair by the window that looked out on nothing, which was the point of the window, and watching the moths with the expression of a person watching a small fire they had once been afraid of. At six she stood. She put the rubber chicken back in the purse, considered it, and left it on the desk. "The biscuits," she said. "There's a tin in the purse. Shortbread. From a woman in Leeds who died in a shopping trolley accident. She'd bought them for her grandson and never got round to them, so I've been holding them for a while, and I've decided you can have them." "Shortbread." "Very good shortbread. Mortal. Unburnt. It's a miracle, technically, that it's still shortbread." She went through the wall the way she came, and the moths drifted toward the lamp in the shape of her absence, and then, as they do, lost the shape and drifted on. Lucifer sat with the ledger and the chicken and the tin of shortbread. He opened the tin. The biscuits were perfect, golden, faintly salted, the smell of them entirely unlike anything in Hell, which was to say the smell of them was like a kitchen, and Hell had no kitchens, and there he was, eating one. He ate a second. He ate a third, and then he stopped, because eating biscuits in order of preference was a habit of a man with nowhere to be, and he was the Devil, and even the Devil had meetings. He stamped the intake forms. He wrote in the ledger: *Day adequate. Screaming adequate. Moths present.* Then he went to the hall and left the lamp on, and the kettle on, and the spare room aired, and he stood for a moment in the doorway of it, listening to the screaming go on below, adequate, adequate, and thought: *she said she wasn't here to talk.* The moths came to him, one at a time, drawn by the lamp he had left burning, and he let them land on his sleeve, and did not brush them off, and went back to his desk, and the night went on in Hell, as nights do, which is to say it went on at all, which was more than could be said for most nights in most places.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the prompt's requirements, successfully merging the mundane bureaucracy of Hell with intimate relationship dynamics. The author captures a distinctly Gaiman-esque voice through understated prose, dry humor, and the treatment of supernatural elements as matter-of-fact administrative concerns. The characterization is particularly strong. Lucifer emerges as a lonely bureaucrat dealing with pension disputes and intake forms, while his longing for Lilith manifests through small domestic details - the aired spare room, the good cup with a chip, the kettle kept warm. These details effectively show rather than tell the emotional state of their relationship. Lilith's characterization through her actions (coming through walls, bringing oddly meaningful gifts) feels authentic to both her mythological nature and the story's tone. The prose style successfully emulates Gaiman's understated irony. Lines like "black was the only colour that didn't have to explain itself" and the description of Astoreth as someone "promoted by mistake" who works with "furious competence" demonstrate the author's skill with dry, observational humor. The bureaucratic absurdities (Charon wanting a pension "in principle," screaming calibrated to "adequate") create effective dark comedy. The imagery is consistently strong without becoming overwrought. The moths serve as a particularly effective recurring motif, representing both domesticity and the delicate nature of the relationship. The description of Hell's administrative machinery feels both fantastical and mundane. The emotional complexity is well-handled. The tentative dance between the characters, their unspoken history, and the careful way they navigate their "off again" status creates genuine tension. The ending, with Lucifer leaving lights on and eating shortbread, strikes an appropriate note of cautious hope without being overly positive. The dialogue, while minimal, feels natural and serves the characters well. Lilith's matter-of-fact explanations and Lucifer's careful responses reveal their dynamic effectively. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the Gaiman pastiche becomes slightly too obvious, and a few descriptions that edge toward being overly precious. The pacing occasionally slows in the middle sections, though this may be intentional to reflect the mundane nature of Hell's daily operations. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
The condemned went out at dawn, before the sun reached the practice yard. I watched them from the doorway of the cella: four men with their hands bound and their heads shaved, being pushed through the gate by the lanista's slaves. One was a baker from the Subura, I knew him by his hands, the flour worked into the creases of his knuckles. He did not look back. The others looked back at nothing in particular. "The morning games are for men the city has already paid for," Priscus said. He was counting something on his fingers, as he always did, as if the dead were a column in a ledger. "You are an investment. Don't waste the morning." So we drilled until the heat rose off the paving stones and the practice swords rang like dishes in a kitchen. Milo swung his rudi at the wooden posts with the carelessness of a man who had been doing it since he was old enough to hold a knife. He was a murmillo from Narbo, and he fought today against a secutor named Crixus, and the crowd had been betting on him since yesterday's fish market, at the price of oil. "Three drachmas on Crixus," he said, wiping his arms with a rag that had been oil longer than it had been cloth. "The crowd loves a man who bleeds on schedule." I worked the net over the low posts, letting it open and close, open and close, until the bronze handle was warm in my palm. The trident weighed seven pounds and I had carried it four years, so I no longer thought of it as heavy. I thought of it as the part of me that remained. From the street came the city's ordinary noise, carts on stone, a dog arguing with a donkey, the fishmongers of the Forum calling their wares, the river's smell coming up through the drains, garum and salt and something rotting sweet. Above it all, faintly, the morning crowd already moving toward the amphitheatre, a sound like a tide that had decided on a direction. At midday the shade came, and with it the talk. Priscus sat on the bench with his oil-stained tunic and his ledger, and he told us what today's games were for. "The emperor's games," he said. "The Dacian games. The treasury is full, and Trajan wants the city to know it." He spat. "There is Dacian gold in the Forum, in the coffer, in the columns. The whole city knows the emperor took Dacia, and the games are his receipt." Milo laughed at this, as if it were a joke about someone else's war. "And you're the receipt's proof," he said, without malice. "They give us bread and a day of screaming, and we give them the rest of the day." He had it right. I had stopped arguing with it years ago, the way you stop arguing with the weight of the net. "The patron watches today," Priscus added, and his voice changed, the way it did when money was in the room. "Senator Lucius, he's in the front tier. A retiarius who falls well, who gives the crowd a good death, he might get the rudis. A retiarius who bores them, he gets sold to the ludus in Capua, where the sand is worse and the doctors are worse and the men are worse." Freedom, if you were lucky, and only if the crowd liked watching you be lucky. The new boy arrived at the third hour, chained between two of the lanista's slaves, his arms raw from the manacles. He was Dacian, and young, and his dialect was the southern one, the one my mother spoke, the one that put the emphasis on the second syllable. I knew it the way I knew my own scars. "Another trophy from the wars," Priscus said, and his voice made the word sound like a price. "The emperor sends us his spoils. Feed him, oil him, teach him the net. He fights in a month." The boy's eyes found mine across the yard. I could see him working out the recognition, the way a man works out the shape of a blade before he knows whether it's meant for him. "Eat," I said, in Dacian. "You will need strength." He looked at me for a long moment, and then he nodded, and that was all. There was nothing else to say that the chains were not already saying. In the evening, after the oil and the figs and the small shrine where the other men prayed to the Lares and Fortuna and whatever Roman gods they had been taught to fear, I did what I do before every fight. I took the pouch from under my pallet. Inside was a pinch of sand from the amphitheatre's floor, taken the first week I arrived, when the lanista still let us carry things in our hands and not yet know better. I went to the corner of the practice yard where the rain pools and the sun never reaches, dug a hole with my thumb, and buried the sand. Then I dug it up and held it in my palm, cool and fine as ground bone. I said to it, in Dacian, to the ground and to Zalmoxis, who does not live in Rome but whom I have never stopped asking: it has held me before. Let it hold me again. If the sand knows me, the crowd will have to learn me slowly. Then I walked to the amphitheatre with the rest of them, Milo ahead of me, the net over my shoulder, the trident across my back. The city had turned out. The velarium was going up over the tiers, the great awning worked by sailors from the fleet, and the crowd poured in through the arches, thousands of them, sweating, perfumed, hungry for blood the way the fishmongers' customers were hungry for dinner. The smell of them reached the gate: unwashed bodies, wine, the roasting meat from the stalls, and under it all the plain animal smell of people packed together in the heat. The trumpets sounded from the top of the amphitheatre, the long notes that meant the games would begin, and the crowd answered with a roar that went through me like a hand through a net, finding the holes, testing them. Priscus caught my arm at the gate. "The crowd has been screaming for you since the morning games," he said. "Don't disappoint them." Milo put his hand on my shoulder. "See you in the morning," he said, which is what you say when you are not sure there will be a morning. The doors opened on the light, and the light opened on me, and I went in carrying my net, my name, and a plain that was no longer mine.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric immersion in the Roman gladiatorial world. The author successfully avoids the obvious combat scene, instead focusing on the quieter moments that reveal character depth and historical context. The first-person narration from a Dacian gladiator provides an authentic outsider's perspective on Roman society. The prose style is notably restrained and literary, with carefully chosen details that build the world effectively. Phrases like "the condemned went out at dawn" and "the dead were a column in a ledger" establish tone efficiently. The sensory details are well-integrated - the smell of garum and salt, the sound of practice swords "like dishes in a kitchen," the tactile weight of the seven-pound trident. The character work is sophisticated, particularly in how the protagonist's Dacian identity creates layers of meaning. His interaction with the new Dacian prisoner is handled with subtle emotion, and his private ritual with the sand reveals spiritual depth without exposition. The supporting characters like Milo and Priscus feel authentic to their roles and time period. The historical elements are woven naturally into the narrative. References to Trajan's Dacian campaigns, the social structure of the ludus, and the economic realities of gladiatorial games demonstrate solid research without feeling forced. The political commentary emerges organically through character observations rather than authorial intrusion. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overly literary language that can feel slightly precious. Some metaphors, while beautiful, may be too modern in sensibility for the character voice. The ending, while poetic, borders on being too consciously artistic. The dialogue is minimal but effective when present, particularly the brief exchange in Dacian. The pacing builds appropriately toward the arena entrance, maintaining tension without relying on action sequences. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**14th October** Ma, The light is burning. The tender came Tuesday with the coal and the Board's letters, and yours, so I know you're well. I wind the clockwork at four and eight and twelve and four again, that's the whole of a day when the sea's flat. When it's not flat it's the whole of a day and then some. The new keeper from the mainland came to see me off in August and stood at the door a long time. I told him the island was bigger than it looks from the sea. He didn't believe me. Yours, Rab **2nd November** Rab, I got your letter and read it twice, that's the truth of it. Dolly's gone to the home at Govanhill, the one by the church, and I'm going too come the first of the month, so we can be on the same floor if the matron allows. I'm not in it for the comfort of it. I'm sending tins of soup and a tin of shortbread, the good kind from the shop on the High Street. Eat them and don't hoard them like your father did. Tell the sea to mind itself. Your Ma **19th November** Ma, The tender missed the week. Then missed the week after. The Board says the weather's the reason, and the weather has opinions. I'm on the soup and the shortbread now, one tin every other day, and the water tank's at the third mark. I've nailed your letters up in the watch room so I've something to read when the lamp needs no watching. Yours, Rab **4th December** Rab, I heard from Dolly the tender's not coming, and I've written to the Company myself. You're not to starve on a rock because some clerk's lazy. Come home for Christmas anyway. There's no light to keep that's worth your bones. Your Ma **22nd December** Ma, I can't come home. There's a light to keep, and you know that better than I do. The Board sent word the light is to be automated come spring. A man from Glasgow will fit the machinery and I'll be stood down. I've kept it burning nine years and it's going to burn without me. I don't know what I'll do with my hands. Yours, Rab **9th January** Rab, Dolly's gone. Passed in her sleep, the matron says, no pain, which is more than I can promise myself. I'm not dying, mind. I'm seventy-one and stubborn as a mule. But I'm tired, Rab. Tired of the quiet floor and the tinned tea. Come home when you can. Your Ma **30th January** Ma, I'm sorry about Dolly. The tender came on the 12th with coal and a crate of tins and a week of letters. Yours were in it, all of them, and I read them in order and cried in the watch room like a boy, which I'm not sorry for. I'm rationing the coal now. I burn the crates when I can. The lamp comes first. Yours, Rab **16th February** Rab, The doctor says I'm to stop fussing and I say the doctor can go to hell. I'm sending the shortbread again. Eat. The light's burning there and I'm burning here, that's the whole of it, and one of us ought to stop, and it's not the light. Come home, bairn. Your Ma **4th March** Ma, There's a trawler off the rocks. Lost her lights in the gale and she's drifting toward them like she means it. I've wound the clockwork twice in an hour and it's still turning, that's the only thing I can do. The radio says she's out of Oban with eleven men aboard. I can't go out. There's no boat here and no one else. So I keep the light burning, and I keep it burning, and I keep it burning. Yours, Rab **20th March** Rab, They've moved me to the quiet floor. I'm not to worry, the matron says, but I'm worrying. Keep the light burning. That's all. Your Ma **11th April** Ma, The tender came and took me. I've been stood down, the machinery's fitted, and I'm in Glasgow now. The trawler made it to shore, they say, all eleven men, and a man from the Board wrote to thank the light. I went to Govanhill on the Saturday. You were in the day room with Dolly's old knitting needles in your lap, and you looked up and said, "So you've come." You looked smaller than in your letters, Ma. We've taken the back room of the house on the High Street, the one Dolly kept for us. There's a stove and a kettle and no clockwork to wind. I think I'll keep this one burning. Yours, Rab **14th April** Rab, The kettle's on. Don't be late. Your Ma

[Analysis] This epistolary narrative successfully fulfills most of the prompt requirements, creating a compelling story through correspondence between Rab, a Scottish lighthouse keeper, and his mother. The piece spans several months and builds to an emotional climax with a satisfying resolution. The characterization is particularly strong. Rab's voice comes through clearly as working-class Scottish, with natural speech patterns like "that's the whole of it" and "mind itself." His dedication to duty and struggle with isolation are well-established. The mother's voice is equally distinct - practical, caring, and increasingly frail, with her own Scottish inflections. The contrast between their personalities creates authentic tension. The gradual plot development works effectively. The story moves from routine isolation through supply disruptions, the announcement of automation, personal loss (Dolly's death), a crisis with the trawler, and finally reunion. Each letter reveals new information while maintaining the characters' distinct voices. The emotional arc is well-constructed. The isolation builds naturally, punctuated by the mother's declining health and Rab's dedication to his duty. The trawler incident serves as an effective climax, demonstrating the real purpose of Rab's sacrifice. The resolution feels earned rather than forced. The prose is generally elegant and restrained, avoiding purple language while maintaining atmospheric quality. Phrases like "I'm burning here, that's the whole of it" and "you looked smaller than in your letters" are particularly effective. The imagery of light and burning creates a subtle thematic thread. However, there are some minor weaknesses. The timeline occasionally feels compressed - major life changes happen quite rapidly. Some transitions between letters could be smoother, and a few moments border on being slightly overwrought, though this is minimal. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - hopeful but not unrealistically positive. Rab's transition from lighthouse keeper to caretaker of his mother feels natural and thematically consistent. The final exchange is touching without being saccharine. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bread basket arrived before I'd finished deciding whether to order. Unattended food, unmonitored table, a kitchen pass wide open. That's how my eyes still work. I'm a pentester now, authorized work: you sign a document saying you're allowed to break things, then you break them carefully and hand someone a PDF. Four years ago I didn't need a document. I don't think about it much, but everything in this restaurant has an attack surface. The barista writing names in marker anyone can read. And June, sitting across from me, who I came here hoping to be a person with and not a target. So far she's ordering the rigatoni and laughing at my firewall jokes, and I'm doing my best to be boring. Then she asks what I actually do, I say security, and her face does the thing where a door opens. "Do you play Magic?" I told her I used to. I quit when I quit offensive work, because I couldn't stand building something just to prove I could take it apart. But I know the cards, like old friends I stopped calling. "I played blue control," she says. "Denial of service. My whole deck is a polite way of saying your plans are cancelled." There it is. Rapport. Two people who speak a language the rest of the restaurant doesn't have. She tells me Force of Will is her card, that she buys every reprint. Force of Will: three mana, deny the thing they're about to do. She's patient. She doesn't commit early; she waits for the opponent to telegraph and then erases it. Noted. She tells me Venser is her favorite card ever, and says it like some people say a pet's name. Counter and bounce. She doesn't just stop your plan, she sends it back to your hand to think about. I'm mapping her, and I hate that I'm doing it, and I can't stop. She's careful, disciplined. She doesn't give out information in the first ten minutes. Doomsday is her dream game, she tells me. Five cards in hand, shuffle the top forty, and if one of them is right, you win. The gambler's control: she wants the endgame perfect but will gamble on a narrow window, only risk she's engineered. She likes card advantage, she says. Ponder is great. Always know more than your opponent. Ponder: look at three cards, keep one, rest on top. She reads before she acts. She tells me she played Dack Fayden once, blue aggro, win fast or lose fast. Dack. She doesn't enjoy losing. A control player who keeps an aggro deck in her back pocket knows her own patience has a limit. She's not a monk. She's a monk with a knife. Then she says Mind Control is the best feeling in the game, grinning. I sit back. Mind Control: take a creature, make it yours, fight with it for a turn. She likes holding other people's plans in her hand. I know what that means. I don't say it. She adds that Cyclonic Rift is so satisfying. Rift: flip everything over, start clean. She likes resets, as long as she pushes the button. I have a complete picture now, flattering and also a dossier. Somewhere between the second and third card I realized I was doing to her what I used to do to systems: catalog, predict, wait for the moment to strike. Except she's a person, eating rigatoni, telling me about reprint announcements. Then her phone buzzes. She unlocks it to check a notification and there it is. The zigzag. Top-left, middle-right, bottom-left, middle-right, bottom-right. The one from the documentary. The one on every list of the five most common Android patterns, brute-forceable
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative understanding of the prompt. The author successfully captures the mindset of a reformed hacker through an internal monologue that feels authentic and psychologically complex. The protagonist's inability to stop analyzing vulnerabilities - both technical and human - creates compelling tension throughout the narrative. The Magic: The Gathering conceit works exceptionally well as both a bonding mechanism and a metaphor for the protagonist's analytical nature. The author shows impressive knowledge of the game, using specific cards to reveal character traits in both the protagonist and their date. This creates layers of meaning where the card discussions serve as both genuine connection and unconscious psychological profiling. The prose is clean and purposeful, with sentences that flow naturally and maintain consistent voice throughout. The internal monologue feels genuine to someone with this technical background, using appropriate jargon without becoming inaccessible. Phrases like "everything in this restaurant has an attack surface" and "I'm mapping her, and I hate that I'm doing it, and I can't stop" effectively convey the protagonist's compulsive analytical nature. The character work is particularly strong. The protagonist emerges as genuinely conflicted - wanting human connection while being unable to suppress their professional instincts. The date, June, becomes a fully realized person through the card discussions rather than remaining a cipher. The author shows rather than tells us about both characters' personalities through their gaming preferences and reactions. However, the piece has some notable weaknesses. It ends abruptly just as the central conflict (the insecure phone pattern) is introduced, failing to deliver on the promised "negotiating the fallout" and attempt to "salvage or sabotage" the date. This feels incomplete rather than artfully open-ended. The piece also occasionally veers toward being overly technical in ways that might alienate readers unfamiliar with either hacking or Magic terminology. The emotional complexity is well-handled, particularly the protagonist's self-awareness about their problematic behavior and their genuine desire to change. The writing avoids cheap sentiment while still creating investment in the character's struggle.
