+ Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The briefing had used the word *unstable* eleven times, *volatile* four, and *insurrectionary* once, and had described the three peoples of Kiln, on the world Cinder, as three weather systems sharing a roof. Nessa had read it twice aboard the transit and begun to believe it, the way you believe a map drawn by frightened men. So when the escort finished its formal visit to the ferry works and turned toward the compound, she walked on. Protocol said guests of the settlement did not walk alone after the second bell. She was past it by a quarter hour, and the market was thickest. The stalls ran down the Low City in two rows, and the first thing she saw was cloth. Handwoven bolts dyed in colours she had no names for: a blue deeper than any indigo Earth had made, a red that seemed to hold warmth in the weave, a green like the inside of a river stone. The dyers worked with plants from the salt flats and the river mud, and their pots smoked in the cold air, and nobody looked at her with fear. A Deep woman sold lengths of the blue beside a High man. The Deep were broad, dark-adapted, lowland folk built for the foundries' gloom. The High were thin and dense, built for plateau air. The briefing had said they did not share tables. They shared this stall, and haggled in a common tongue neither had learned from the other. Their children played in the same dust. Between the stalls moved the Lineage, the founding families, in Earth-cut coats, speaking the old tongue, regarding the other two peoples the way old-country cousins regard new-country ones. Nessa did not go far before she found the uglier half of the briefing, true after all. At the ferry landing, a queue of Deep folk stood apart from the High, and a warden with a ledger turned some away, one by one, without raising his voice. Something was wrong here. It was not insurrection. It was a ledger, kept wrong, or kept to be wrong. She stood in the queue as any citizen would, and was allowed to cross. The reprimand came on the comm lamp while she was still in her corridor. Command was brief, which meant it was serious. "You left your escort. You are a guest of the settlement, not a tourist of it. Tomorrow you will see the Minister of Science, at the hour she chooses, and you will speak of the transit works and nothing else." The Minister of Science was a political posting; the briefing had flagged her plainly. A career administrator, fifteen years stationed, her portfolio the census, the schools, the water shares. Her science was her office, not her practice. Minister Rho received her in a cold room with a map of the transit works on the wall and tea that tasted of nothing. "You walked the market," the Minister said. It was not a question. "I did." "Against protocol." "I was told to speak of the transit works and nothing else. The market is not a transit work, so I have nothing to report on it." Rho let the silence sit where she had put it, then poured the nothing-tea into a second cup and pushed it across. "Command sent you to assess instability. Eleven times the word, I understand." "Eleven." "And what did you find?" Nessa had prepared, on the walk back, a safe version of the truth: friction, minor, manageable. She looked at the ferry line running through the map like a seam, and said what she had seen instead. "I found a market where two peoples trade cloth dyed in pigments Earth has never made. I found their children in the same dust. And I found a ferry warden keeping a ledger that turns Deep folk away while High folk cross free." "Go on." "The tensions are real. They are small. A ledger, water shares, a school that teaches one language and not the other. Command's fear is bigger than all of them together, and fear travels faster than ferries." Rho studied her. Grey-haired, careful-handed, a woman who had signed a great many documents. "You are young," she said. "You will be recalled in a year. Command will read your report and decide Cinder is a problem to manage or a problem to suppress, and either way you go home to write it." "Either way, it will be a true report, or it won't. I have seen both kinds of envoy come through here. I would rather be the one who comes back changed." "Changed," Rho said. "A dangerous word for a diplomat." "I would rather be wrong on purpose than right by accident." Something moved in the Minister's face, the loosening of a held position. She took the map down and unrolled a second, older, with the ferry line struck through and redrawn. "The warden's name is Osk. The ledger is his, and it is wrong, and the council has known for two years because the council fears the High wardens' guild. Carry that to Command as a transit failure, a broken ferry system. That is within your mandate." "And the truth of the peoples?" "The truth of the peoples is that they are not Earth's peoples, and they are not the same as one another, and they are not the monsters your briefing made of them. That truth is mine to manage. It does not need a young woman's courage. It needs a young woman's ear." "Then give me the census. And the water-share records. And tell the council a guest of Command has asked to observe the fourth's sitting." "You will sit where guests sit. You will say nothing. Then we will talk about what you saw." Nessa left the cold room with the census figures pressed flat in her coat and a length of the deep blue cloth under her arm, bought from the stall on her way out, paid for with a month of ration credit. It was the first thing she owned on Cinder, and the first thing she had chosen for herself.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Le Guin's distinctive style, particularly her anthropological approach to science fiction and her spare, precise prose. The author successfully creates a complex colonial society with three distinct human subspecies while avoiding heavy-handed exposition. The worldbuilding feels organic, revealed through concrete details like the ferry system, market interactions, and administrative structures. The characterization is particularly strong. Nessa emerges as a believable diplomatic envoy - curious, principled, but not naively idealistic. Her decision to break protocol feels earned rather than contrived. Minister Rho is expertly crafted as a seasoned political operator who tests Nessa's mettle through careful verbal sparring rather than obvious confrontation. The dialogue between them crackles with subtext and political maneuvering. The prose style authentically captures Le Guin's voice - economical yet evocative, with careful attention to concrete details that illuminate larger themes. Phrases like "a map drawn by frightened men" and "fear travels faster than ferries" demonstrate sophisticated metaphorical thinking. The author avoids purple prose while maintaining rich descriptive passages, particularly in the market scene. The political complexity feels genuine rather than simplistic. The tensions between the three peoples are neither overblown nor dismissed, and the administrative corruption (the ferry ledger) provides a concrete manifestation of systemic problems. The resolution avoids both cynicism and false optimism - Nessa gains access to information and a path forward, but the fundamental challenges remain. The pacing is well-controlled, moving from exploration to confrontation to negotiation without feeling rushed. The ending strikes an appropriate note - progress without transformation, understanding without resolution. The symbolic purchase of the blue cloth provides a nice concrete detail that suggests Nessa's growing connection to this world without being heavy-handed. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the political dynamics could be even more nuanced, and occasionally the dialogue, while strong, doesn't quite reach Le Guin's level of subtlety. The piece also might benefit from slightly more sensory detail in places to fully immerse the reader. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Polymerase Chain Reaction** The thermal cycler was a Helixion unit with a rice cooker's guts, wired to a car battery through a salvaged oven thermostat, and it worked. That was the whole argument for keeping it. I set the sample on the block and watched the display climb. Denature at ninety-four. Anneal at fifty-five. Extend at seventy-two. Polymerase chain reaction, the old textbooks called it, which was a polite name for what I was actually doing: copying a handful of surviving wild-type genes out of seed stock that had been rotting since the companies died, before the last copies of them rotted too. The tiles under my boots were cracked, and in the cracks the mushrooms grew. Glow mushrooms, pale green, from some abandoned splicing test. Nobody had ever licensed them. That was why they were still here, thirty years after Helixion's campus went quiet, while everything else engineered in this building had expired like milk. The mushrooms had been the last thing they tested before they left, and they'd never gotten the tag. I pulled the sample tube. Three copies of the wild gene, maybe four, amplified from a smear of dead seed. Enough. On the shelf behind me stood the rye I'd spliced for the Hollow's spring planting, third generation, still green, still alive in a world that had taught everything to die on schedule. The knock came at dusk. Three sharp raps, the broker's knock. Osei stood in the doorway with a crate on her back and a girl behind her who walked like her bones were a rumor. "Contract," Osei said. She set the crate down and counted the Hollow's needs out loud, because she was the kind of woman who did arithmetic in front of witnesses. Two crates of wild seed stock, rye and amaranth, never touched by Helixion's pens. One crate of antibiotics with real dates on them. In exchange: her daughter spliced. And the method. "Your daughter has the drift," I said. It wasn't a question. June was fourteen, maybe. Her hair had gone thin and grey. Her skin was translucent over the knuckles, veins like blue threads under wax paper. Engineered people were supposed to last one generation, then their cells forgot the instructions. The drift. Most of them just died quiet. "The method," Osei said again. "The vector. Your settlement's got grain problems too, Wren. Everyone knows you're splicing wild genes into the Hollow's wheat. I'm offering the seed stock that could end that." I looked at the girl's hands. I looked at the mushrooms in the tile cracks, the only things in this lab that had outlived a corporation. "Antibiotics and seed stock," I said. "That's the contract." Osei's jaw set. "The vector." "Antibiotics and seed stock. She goes in the lab tonight." The splice took four hours and cost me a hand. The centrifuge was a washing machine drum on a drill, and when the drill slipped, the drum flew and took a strip of my palm with it. I bled for a long time because of my own old splice, a repair enzyme I'd put in myself years back. Fast healing, slow clotting, bruises like a peach. I bandaged it with a strip of lab coat and kept working, because June was asleep on the bench and the spore culture was waiting. The vector was the mushrooms. I'd spent three years growing them, coaxing the wild repair gene into their fruiting bodies. A modified fungal spore, aerosolized into the lungs, carrying the gene like a letter into a house with no address. Untested. I'd told Osei that. She'd signed anyway. June burned for two days. She shook so hard the blankets couldn't hold her, and the second night she said words that weren't hers, which is what the drift does to people, their cells forgetting, their voices too. I ran her fever with the new antibiotics, which worked better than anything in the Hollow's stores, and I sat with my bleeding hand in a bowl of water and let the repair gene do its slow work. On the third morning she woke up white-haired. All of it, silver as seed down. "Look," she said, and her eyes were catching light that wasn't there. She was looking at the Helixion wheat on the shelf, the stock that went sterile by the second generation, and seeing the ghost codes in it, the expiry markers Helixion had built into their property, fluorescing faint red through the husks, the way she could see the mushrooms' green. The vector had given her something nobody had predicted. A way to read the rot coming. I tested her on a rye head from Osei's own crate. She held it to the window light and told me exactly which kernels were wild and which had been touched. "Good girl," I said, and meant it. By the time she could read the Helixion tags off a dead husk, I'd already decided what I was selling. Osei came in at noon, expecting a lecture and getting a result instead. She looked at June's hair. She looked at the wheat. She said, "The method." I handed her a crate. Inside: a spore culture of the mushroom vector, grown fresh, healthy, ready to carry whatever genes she wanted to carry to whoever would pay for them. Before I sealed it, June read me the expiry tag off a dead wheat husk, letter by letter, and I wrote it into the culture's backbone. Osei took it with a handshake and a price for the next shipment of antibiotics, and I watched her go. Then I went to my notes and wrote down what I'd done, which was nothing new in this world. I'd given her a one-generation product. The vector in that crate was spliced to expire after a single pass, the way Helixion had spliced everything they ever sold. Osei would save her settlements' children, and then the method would rot in her hands, and they would have to come back to me, or find someone else who still remembered how to copy a dying gene. The mushrooms grew in the tile cracks while I worked, patient and unlicensed, glowing their small green light in the dark.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk story demonstrates strong technical execution and worldbuilding within the specified parameters. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic setting where corporate genetic engineering with built-in obsolescence has collapsed civilization, leaving survivors to work with degrading genetic material. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, with vivid details like the jury-rigged thermal cycler made from a rice cooker and car battery, and the glowing mushrooms growing in tile cracks - unlicensed organisms that survived because they were never given expiration tags. The scientific elements feel grounded and believable, from PCR amplification to fungal vectors. The protagonist Wren is well-characterized through actions and internal monologue rather than exposition. The physical toll of genetic modification is shown through Wren's own splice that causes slow clotting, and June's transformation from drift victim to someone who can see genetic markers is both surprising and logically consistent with the established science. The black market contract plot unfolds naturally, with Osei seeking both treatment for her daughter and the method itself. The story's central irony - that Wren gives Osei a one-generation vector, perpetuating the same planned obsolescence that caused the apocalypse - is both thematically resonant and morally complex. The prose is lean and atmospheric, with strong imagery like June's "bones were a rumor" and veins "like blue threads under wax paper." The voice remains consistent throughout, maintaining a clinical yet empathetic tone that suits both the scientific subject matter and post-apocalyptic setting. The dialogue serves multiple functions efficiently, revealing character relationships, advancing plot, and establishing the transactional nature of this world. The ending avoids false optimism while providing a satisfying resolution that comments on cycles of exploitation. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the scientific exposition could flow more naturally, and the transformation of June, while earned through the established science, happens quite rapidly. However, these don't significantly detract from an otherwise accomplished piece.
